books.title: Hubble: An Out-of-This-World Telescope
books.art_why: Keyword check recommends drawing for this illustrated space book.

pages.text: Introduction Look into the sky on a clear night. That multitude of stars is what the Hubble Space Telescope sees all the time, only better. The Hubble Telescope doesn’t sit on the ground. It orbits Earth, circling high above the planet’s atmosphere. The atmosphere is very important to life on Earth, but the atmosphere causes problems for telescopes. It blocks out some kinds of light, which is what makes stars look as though they twinkle. Astronomers solved the problem of having to look through the atmosphere to study objects in space by launching the Hubble Space Telescope. Because the Hubble is outside the atmosphere, it can see objects more clearly than telescopes on Earth.
pages.brief: The Hubble Space Telescope orbits high above Earth, circling beyond the planet’s atmosphere. Below it, Earth’s atmosphere glows around the planet, while a clear night sky filled with a multitude of stars stretches beyond. The telescope looks outward, showing why it sees space more clearly than ground telescopes.

pages.text: Hubble’s New Eyes The Hubble is one of the best telescopes astronomers have. The telescope’s images show stars forming, stars dying, and the universe expanding. Recently, astronauts visited the Hubble in space to install new equipment. With the new instruments in place, the Hubble can see better than ever.
pages.brief: Astronauts in space suits work outside the Hubble Space Telescope to install new equipment. The telescope floats above Earth, its instruments open to the stars. Around it, the dark sky suggests the stars and universe the Hubble observes, now with better views than before.

pages.text: Nancy Grace Roman: Mother of Hubble Doctor Nancy Grace Roman, NASA’s first chief astronomer, is often called the “Mother of Hubble.” She believed in the Hubble telescope project from the beginning, and she was able to convince many other scientists to believe in it as well. As a young girl, Nancy was drawn to studying the stars and space. She knew early on that she wanted to be an astronomer; she even formed an astronomy club with her friends at school. She also knew that her dream would take years of hard work to achieve and that there were not many women in the field of astronomy—but she was up for the challenge!
pages.brief: A young Nancy Grace Roman stands with school friends in an astronomy club, looking at stars and space. She is drawn to studying the sky and already dreams of becoming an astronomer. The group is at school, with Nancy focused on the stars above.

pages.text: In 1949, Roman earned her doctorate. Ten years later and just six months after NASA was formed, she went to work there. While at NASA, Dr. Roman successfully created a team of engineers and astronomers to envision what would become the Hubble Telescope. She convinced NASA and Congress that for a small tax that would cost Americans no more than the price of one night at the movies, they would get fifteen years of amazing discoveries! NASA has named a space telescope after Dr. Roman because of her amazing contributions to the scientific community. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, or Roman Space Telescope for short, will launch in the mid-2020s. It will search for distant planets and study the history of the universe.
pages.brief: Dr. Nancy Grace Roman stands with a team of engineers and astronomers at NASA, discussing plans for a large space telescope. She presents the project to NASA and Congress. Nearby, the planned Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is shown as a future telescope that will search for distant planets and study the universe’s history.

pages.text: Carina Nebula: A Star Nursery One of the Hubble’s new cameras takes amazing pictures of baby stars. (Astronomers use this term for new stars, even though they know stars are not actually born.) Stars form in clouds of spinning gas such as those found in many nebulas. The Carina Nebula is a cloud of dust and gas in space that gives scientists a chance to see stars forming.
pages.brief: The Carina Nebula glows as a huge cloud of dust and gas in space, with baby stars forming inside it. The Hubble’s new camera captures the cloudy nursery, where spinning gas gives scientists a chance to see stars beginning to grow.

pages.text: The Carina Nebula has huge plumes of dust. Some of them cover more than three hundred light years of space. One light year is the distance light travels in one year—so it would take three hundred years for light to travel across the nebula. The Carina Nebula also has a large collection of stars. Those stars pull on each other and move the cloud of dust around. Astronomers love to look at this changing nebula. Before the Hubble’s new camera was installed, they knew the Carina Nebula was forming stars, but they couldn’t see the actual process. Once the new camera was installed, astronomers focused it on the nebula. They used visible light to take pictures that show the dark, swirling dust. Then astronomers changed the camera to view infrared light. Infrared is a type of light humans cannot see. When the camera takes infrared pictures, the computer colors the image with “false” colors so people can see them. The infrared camera looked right through the clouds of dust to see the gases spinning at over 1.3 million kilometers per hour (850,000 mph). These swirlings are baby stars that are just starting to grow.
pages.brief: The Carina Nebula shows dark, swirling dust plumes stretching across space, with stars pulling the cloud around. Seen in visible light, the dust is dark; in infrared, false colors reveal the hot gases spinning at over 1.3 million kilometers per hour, where baby stars are beginning to grow.

pages.text: Different Kinds of Energy Light is a kind of energy that moves in waves. Scientists measure it in wavelengths, or the distance from the top of one wave to the top of the next wave. Humans can see the energy called visible light, but there are many other kinds of energy we can’t see. Gamma rays, X-rays, and ultraviolet light have shorter wavelengths than visible light. Infrared, microwave, and radio energy have longer wavelengths than visible light. Most telescopes are designed to “see” only one or two of these energy types. The Hubble is unusual in that it can measure ultraviolet, visible, and even some of the infrared wavelengths. Combining these different views into one picture can produce incredibly beautiful and informative images of objects in our universe.
pages.brief: Ribbons of energy ripple through space in different wavelengths, some short and some long, with visible light among them. The Hubble Space Telescope gathers ultraviolet, visible, and some infrared views, combining them into a single colorful image of an object in the universe.

pages.text: Omega Centauri: A Globular Cluster Astronomers pointed the upgraded Hubble Space Telescope at Omega Centauri, a huge group of stars—ten million or more. When that many stars group together in space, we call them a globular cluster. Omega Centauri was a place where the Hubble had looked before. But now, with the new instruments installed, astronomers hoped to learn even more. The cluster shows stars in different age groups. Most of the stars start out yellow, like our sun. As they get older, they balloon out, becoming larger and red. In the last phase, the stars turn blue. These dying stars are smaller and hotter than the others.
pages.brief: Omega Centauri appears as a huge globular cluster, packed with ten million or more stars. The upgraded Hubble looks at the cluster, where stars show different ages: many start yellow like the sun, older ones balloon into red, and dying stars turn small, hot blue.

pages.text: The new images may hold the clue to a mystery. Scientists say that some of the pictures show a blank spot. The stars around the blank spot look as though they are being pulled inside. That blank spot might be a black hole—a kind of vacuum in space. Because black holes generate amazing amounts of gravity, they would pull hard on the stars. Scientists think the presence of a black hole would help explain why the stars stayed together in a cluster.
pages.brief: Inside the star cluster Omega Centauri, a dark blank spot appears among the stars. The surrounding stars look as though they are being pulled inward toward it. Scientists think the blank spot might be a black hole, whose strong gravity would pull on the stars and help keep the cluster together.

pages.text: Stephan’s Quintet The five galaxies in Stephan’s Quintet appear to be fighting. The Hubble’s improved equipment better shows how the galaxies are pulling on each other and have grown loops and tails instead of having the normal rounded shape. This tug of war happens when galaxies are close to each other. Eventually, at least one of the galaxies will get pulled into another one. However, their collision will not make a loud crash because sound does not travel through the emptiness of space.
pages.brief: Five galaxies in Stephan’s Quintet appear to be fighting, pulling on one another with loops and tails instead of normal rounded shapes. The Hubble’s improved equipment shows their close tug of war. At least one galaxy will eventually be pulled into another, but the collision makes no loud crash in empty space.

pages.text: Moving stars are silent, but their effects can be dramatic. When a star moves, it creates a bow shock. A bow shock is the energy from an object pushing forward. This energy is like a bow wave that a ship makes as it moves through the water. The larger the ship, the bigger the bow wave. Since stars are huge, their bow shocks can affect objects far away. Scientists say that the Hubble’s improved view of Stephan’s Quintet may help them understand what happened when the universe was young, some fourteen billion years ago. Back then, more stars were close together, so more collisions took place—and many more bow shocks formed.
pages.brief: A star moves through space and creates a bow shock, an energy wave like the bow wave of a ship moving through water. The star’s huge bow shock can affect objects far away. The Hubble’s view of Stephan’s Quintet helps scientists understand the young universe, when stars were closer together and collisions formed many bow shocks.

pages.text: Butterfly Nebula The updated Hubble Space Telescope also took amazing images of the Butterfly Nebula, such as the one on the following page. If you think the Butterfly Nebula looks fragile, look again. Those soft wings are actually super-hot gas. The gas is shooting out of a star in the center. The “wings” of the Butterfly Nebula’s gas cloud stretch more than two light years across. Astronomers say the Butterfly Nebula is both lovely and informative. The nebula is caused by a dying star. The star was once about five times the size of our sun. However, it has been ejecting gas and shrinking for the last 2,200 years. Scientists say our sun might die in the same manner in another five billion years. Astronomers are also watching this nebula to learn more about how the universe recycles. The gases do not just float forever in space; they get used again. The Butterfly Nebula’s clouds contain the elements hydrogen, helium, and carbon. These elements will all eventually become part of a new star or a new planet. In fact, the carbon that helps make up every person on Earth was once part of a star.
pages.brief: The Butterfly Nebula spreads soft-looking wings of super-hot gas shooting out from a dying star at its center. The gas cloud stretches more than two light years across. The star has been ejecting gas and shrinking, and its clouds hold hydrogen, helium, and carbon that will become part of new stars or planets.

pages.text: An exploding star left behind this massive cloud of gas and dust. Chemical “Fingerprints” in Space Space is not empty. Gas, dust, planets, and stars all make up a cosmic web. Astronomers use new instruments on the Hubble to map the universe. The Hubble uses two spectrographs to identify different kinds of matter in space. Using the measurements, astronomers learn four things about each object they observe. They learn the temperature of the object, its density (how “solid” it is), the chemical elements it contains, and how fast it is moving.
pages.brief: A massive cloud of gas and dust left behind by an exploding star fills space. Astronomers use new Hubble instruments to map the universe and identify matter. The Hubble’s two spectrographs measure each object, revealing its temperature, density, chemical elements, and how fast it moves.

pages.text: The spectrographs measure the light that bounces off the gases and dust. Each chemical element looks different from the others. Hydrogen looks different from helium, helium looks different from nitrogen, and so on. Also, warmer objects look different from colder ones. Solid objects look different from gases, and faster objects look different from slower ones. The information these instruments produce does not look like the pictures of the nebula or the globular cluster. This information is presented as a series of lines that are a sort of chemical “fingerprint.” The lines show how much hydrogen, helium, and other matter is in one spot in space. Spectrograph Results Spectrograph target Brightness The Hubble used its spectrograph to study the cloud left behind by an exploding star. Wavelength.
pages.brief: A spectrograph measures light from a target cloud left by an exploding star. Instead of a picture, the result appears as a series of bright and dark lines, like a chemical fingerprint, showing how much hydrogen, helium, and other matter is present in one spot in space.

pages.text: History of the Hubble Space Telescope Astronomers first started using the Hubble to peer into the universe in 1990. When it was first released into orbit from the cargo bay of the shuttle Discovery, people were excited about the possibilities. However, there was a big glitch. The telescope’s main mirror had a tiny imperfection. The mirror is used to collect and focus light on the instruments. The mirror was off by 1/50th of the thickness of a piece of paper. That amount was enough to make the telescope’s images look blurry and slightly out of focus.
pages.brief: The space shuttle Discovery opens its cargo bay and releases the Hubble Space Telescope into orbit in 1990. The telescope’s main mirror has a tiny imperfection—off by 1/50th the thickness of a piece of paper—so its first images look blurry and slightly out of focus.

pages.text: In 1993, astronauts flew to the Hubble and repaired it. After that, the images surprised everyone. No one knew that the telescope would be a source of so much information and beauty. Astronauts visited the telescope four more times. They updated its equipment, proving that astronauts could do complex work in space. With its new equipment installed in 2009, the Hubble looks deeper into the universe than ever before. It can see stars that are dying and stars that are just starting out. Understanding how the universe is put together will help people travel through space. It will also help people who hope to find life on other planets. With its new computers and batteries, the Hubble is expected to continue working for many more years. NASA launched the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) at the end of 2021.
pages.brief: Astronauts repair the Hubble Space Telescope during a spacewalk in 1993, and its images surprise everyone. Later visits update its equipment, and in 2009 new instruments let Hubble look deeper at dying and newborn stars. At the end of 2021, NASA launches the James Webb Space Telescope.

pages.text: A “Cool” Future: The James Webb Space Telescope The JWST is cool in more ways than one; engineers have designed the JWST to make sure that the telescope will not heat up in space. If the telescope gets too warm, it won’t pick up tiny levels of infrared light. Engineers have built a sun shield the size of a tennis court that will keep the telescope in the shade so it will stay cool enough to do its job.
pages.brief: The James Webb Space Telescope floats in space with a giant sun shield the size of a tennis court. Engineers designed the shield to keep the telescope in the shade and cool, so it will not heat up and can pick up tiny levels of infrared light.

pages.text: The new telescope is bigger than the Hubble and lighter. The whole JWST, including the giant sun shield, was folded up to squeeze into a five- meter cargo bay and then unfolded in space. Once there, it began its job of taking a long, deep look at our universe.
pages.brief: The James Webb Space Telescope is bigger than the Hubble but lighter. Folded up with its giant sun shield, it fits into a five-meter cargo bay, then unfolds in space. Once unfolded, it begins taking a long, deep look at the universe.

books.title: Pirate Ships and Flags
books.art_why: Historical pirate periods and ancient ships are before photography, so drawings fit.

pages.text: Early ships were not as large or as fast as most of the ships that were used in the 1700s. This was the Golden Age of piracy (1650s–1730s). As you read, you will learn about different types of pirate ships and life on these ships. You will also read about pirate attacks.
pages.brief: A small early oared ship and a larger 1700s sailing ship are shown on open water, with pirate crewmen aboard. The older ship looks slower and less seaworthy than the bigger vessel, setting up a comparison of ships across the Golden Age of piracy.

pages.text: Greek and Roman Pirate Ships Some early pirates came out of the ancient Greek and Roman empires. They did their pirating over 1,500 years ago. The sea around Greece is filled with many small islands. Ships carrying valuables sailed between the islands. They traveled close to the shore. This made it easy for the pirates who were hiding on the islands. The Greek pirates used streamlined ships for their attacks. These ships were called galleys. These sleek ships were powered by oars. Some also had one or two large sails. Depending on the size of the pirate ship, dozens of pirate crewmen rowed the ship. A galley under the power of many oars was much faster than the clumsy cargo ships that depended on wind power. A galley could quickly overtake a slower cargo ship.
pages.brief: In the sea around Greece, a sleek Greek pirate galley rows out from a cluster of small islands. Dozens of crewmen pull long oars while a single large sail catches the wind. The galley closes in on a clumsy, wind-powered cargo ship carrying valuables near the shore.

pages.text: Galleys were also shallow. This made them easier to steer. They could quickly change direction. It also meant that if the pirates were being chased, they could escape to shallow water. They could also go over rocks that large ships would get caught on. These pirate ships often had sharp battering rams attached to the bow, or front of the ship. They would ram the victim ship, trying to punch a hole in its side, or hull. If the ship being attacked took on water, it became even slower. T he e yes h ave I T Roman pirate ships often had eyes painted on both sides of the bow. The pirates claimed the eyes helped them find their victims. The idea of painting eyes on ships probably came from Egypt, where the eyes were thought to bring good luck.
pages.brief: A shallow pirate galley steers through rocky shallows, its long oars letting it turn quickly. At the bow, a sharp battering ram points toward the hull of a victim ship. Painted eyes stare from both sides of the Roman-style bow as the galley moves in to attack.

pages.text: Romans were not natural seafarers like the Greeks. So they built many of their ships to copy the Greeks. Roman pirates also used galleys powered by long oars. Some of these galleys had rowers at more than one level of the ship. The poor oarsmen who rowed below the deck were forced to row where it was hot and stinky. T he s eIzure of C aesar In about 75 bce, when Julius Caesar was young, he was captured by pirates while on his way to Rhodes to study. He was held for five weeks until his ransom was paid. He later tracked down his captors and had them killed.
pages.brief: A Roman-style galley moves under long oars, with rowers working on more than one level. Below deck, hot and tired oarsmen pull in cramped conditions. Young Julius Caesar is shown as a captive of pirates, waiting during his five weeks of captivity.

pages.text: Viking Pirate Ships While the Greek and Roman pirates threatened ships sailing around southern Europe, the Vikings—most active from 800 ce to 1100 ce— ruled the seas of northern Europe. The Viking pirates were ruthless villains of the north. They attacked ships at sea as well as villages along the coast. These people of the north gained a reputation for being fierce warriors. Vikings were also expert shipbuilders. The seas of northern Europe were often very rough, unlike the smoother waters of the Mediterranean. The ships used by Viking pirates had to be strong so that they would not break up in the rugged sea. Their ships were known as longboats.
pages.brief: In the rough seas of northern Europe, Viking pirates sail strong, sturdy longboats. The fierce warriors attack a coastal village and a ship at sea, showing their reputation as ruthless raiders of the north. Their shipbuilding skill keeps the longboats from breaking apart in the rugged water.

pages.text: Longboats were long, as their name suggests. They were also narrow and sleek. This made them fast and easy to steer. They were powered by a large square sail when in the open sea. When near the shore or going up rivers, they were powered by oars. The longboats were shallow and could land almost anywhere. This made it easy for Viking pirates to sneak up on ships and villages and quickly attack. Longboats were also unique for their design. The front and back of the longboat curved upward to a point. It was difficult to tell the front from the back. The point, or prow, was often decorated with a dragon’s head. These boats were called dragon boats. Other prows were shaped like snake heads or the heads of other figures. Longboats could hold over fifty Viking pirates. These pirates carried spears, axes, swords, and bows and arrows to use in their attacks.
pages.brief: A long, narrow Viking longboat glides near a shore, its shallow hull letting it land almost anywhere. A square sail is raised for open water, but oars are ready for rivers. A carved dragon’s head rises from the prow, and over fifty pirates aboard carry spears, axes, swords, and bows.

pages.text: Pirate Ships of Northern Africa Another group of pirates did their pirating along the northern coast of Africa a little over 1,000 years ago. These pirates were known as Barbary corsairs. Corsairs used sleek galleys much like the ones used by the Greek and Roman pirates. The oars were rowed by enslaved people, which meant more pirates ended up joining the fighting.
pages.brief: Along the northern coast of Africa, Barbary corsair galleys glide over the water. Enslaved rowers pull the long oars while armed pirates stand ready to join the fighting. The sleek ships resemble the galleys used by Greek and Roman pirates, moving quickly toward their target.

pages.text: The corsairs’ ships were fast. Enslaved people scraped and waxed the hull of their galley between trips at sea. This increased the ship’s speed. The galleys were powered by both oars and sails. The oars were long and heavy. A single oar might have to be rowed by several people. A corsair galley could have two to three masts, each holding a sail of a different size. A corsair galley often held over one hundred people. This meant that trips to sea had to be short, since the galley could not carry enough food and water for long trips. Some corsair galleys were beautiful ships. They were often painted with gold decorations, and gold-painted figures often extended from the back of the ship.
pages.brief: A fast Barbary corsair galley carries over one hundred people, with two or three masts holding sails of different sizes. Long, heavy oars are pulled by several enslaved rowers each. Gold-painted figures extend from the back of the beautiful ship, while workers scrape and wax its hull between trips.

pages.text: Chinese Pirate Ships The seas and coastline of China and southeast Asia were perfect settings for pirates. Chinese pirates hid in mangrove swamps that lined the coast. Chinese pirate captains often led fleets of small pirate ships. One pirate commander, Ching-Chi-ling, led a fleet of nearly 1,000 heavily armed ships. D o y ou K now? Pirates usually threatened coastal villages with destruction and enslavement if the occupants did not pay the pirates large sums of money.
pages.brief: Chinese pirate ships hide among mangrove swamps lining the coast of China and southeast Asia. Ching-Chi-ling, a pirate commander, leads a huge fleet of nearly 1,000 heavily armed ships. From the water, pirates threaten a coastal village with destruction and enslavement unless the occupants pay large sums of money.

pages.text: Larger Chinese pirate ships were called junks. These junks were often converted cargo ships. This meant that they were slower than most other pirate ships, but what these ships lacked in speed they made up in arms. They carried over a dozen large guns. They were such good fighting ships that the Chinese navy could not defeat them. Pirate junks often had three masts. The sails were large and had four sides. They were made of silk reinforced with strips of bamboo. These ships were large enough to provide the captain with a nice place to stay, but the crew lived below in the crowded hold.
pages.brief: A large Chinese junk sails with three masts and big four-sided sails made of silk reinforced with bamboo strips. The converted cargo ship carries over a dozen large guns and proves too strong for the Chinese navy. The captain rests in a nice cabin while the crew lives below in a crowded hold.

pages.text: Pirate Ships of the Caribbean.
pages.brief: Several pirate ships sail across clear blue Caribbean water near low tropical islands. Their sails are full as they move together in a small fleet. The warm sea and scattered islands make a setting suited to Caribbean pirates.

pages.text: P IraTe ’ s s hIP Early pirate ships were small, fast, and usually powered by oars. In the 1700s, that changed. Many pirate ships began to use wind power. Large warships called galleons became popular with pirates. Today, many people think of galleons as pirate ships. A galleon.
pages.brief: A large 1700s galleon sails on the open sea, its many sails filled with wind. This wind-powered warship has become the popular image of a pirate ship. Nearby, a smaller, earlier oared pirate ship shows how pirate vessels were once small, fast, and powered by rowers.

pages.text: P IraTe P aIr This is the flag of “Calico” Jack Rackham, who was married to another famous pirate, Anne Bonny. Most pirates were men, but some were women. Some of these pirates, like Anne Bonny, disguised themselves as men because often women weren’t allowed on pirate ships. Pirate Flags Pirate ships flew flags to warn other ships that they were about to be attacked and that they should surrender. Flags were used to strike fear in the crew of ships about to be attacked. Some flags carried scarier messages than others. For example, an all-red flag signaled certain death. However, sometimes pirates were sneaky. They would sail a friendly flag first. Then when they got close to the ship they were attacking, they would raise the pirate flag. The best-known pirate flag was the Jolly Roger. It was decorated with a skull and two crossed swords, or crossbones. It told crew members on a ship being attacked to surrender without a fight or face death.
pages.brief: A pirate ship flies a black flag with a skull and crossed swords while another raises a plain red flag. Anne Bonny, disguised as a man, stands beside the flag of Calico Jack Rackham. A friendly flag is lowered as a pirate flag rises before an attack.

pages.text: In addition to skulls, bones, and swords, pirate flags were decorated with hourglasses, skeletons, and blood. The hourglass signaled that time was running out and the crew should surrender. One of the most notorious pirates of all time was Blackbeard. Blackbeard’s flag was a skeleton that looked like a devil. The skeleton held a spear that pointed at a red heart. Drops of blood dripped from the heart.
pages.brief: Several pirate flags are shown with hourglasses, skeletons, and drops of blood. One flag bears an hourglass warning that time is running out. Blackbeard’s flag shows a devil-like skeleton holding a spear pointed at a red heart, with blood dripping from the heart.

pages.text: C hIng s hIh A Chinese woman named Zheng Yi Sao, also known as Ching Shih, was one of the most famous woman pirates. After her husband died in 1807, she took over a fleet of 1,800 ships and some 80,000 men (and probably a few women). She led with a strict set of rules and commanded respect. After a successful three years pirating, she retired in 1810 after receiving an offer of pardon from the Chinese government. Ching Shih lived another 34 years and died at age 69.
pages.brief: Zheng Yi Sao, also known as Ching Shih, stands on the deck of a Chinese pirate ship and commands a vast fleet of 1,800 ships and 80,000 men. She leads with strict rules and earns respect. After three successful years, she accepts a pardon and retires.

pages.text: Life on a Pirate Ship.
pages.brief: A pirate crew is shown going about ordinary daily life aboard their ship. Pirates stand on the crowded deck among ropes, sails, and wooden timbers, while others rest or work below. The scene presents the cramped, busy setting where pirates lived at sea.

pages.text: Pirate ships usually had a population of rats. The rats chewed sails and ropes and ate food supplies. Rats were even known to chew through a ship’s hull and sink a ship. Food aboard a pirate ship was repetitive. They had little fresh meat. When they did, it was usually turtle meat. Sometimes pirates ate fresh fish. Otherwise meals consisted of dry, salted meat and dry biscuits, washed down with beer, wine, or water. Ships usually had poor cooking facilities. Pirates ate from metal plates. If they were lucky, they had a fork or spoon. Otherwise they just used their fingers. D o y ou K now? Sometimes chickens were kept aboard the ship. They provided a supply of eggs and fresh meat. Fresh fruit, especially limes, were taken on long voyages to prevent diseases such as scurvy. The fruit gave sailors much-needed vitamin C.
pages.brief: Rats scurry through a pirate ship’s stores, chewing sails, ropes, and food supplies. Pirates eat dry salted meat and biscuits from metal plates, using fingers or a lucky spoon. Chickens are kept for eggs and meat, and limes are stored to prevent scurvy on long voyages.

pages.text: Conclusion Pirate life often looks exciting and full of adventure in the movies. Life aboard a real pirate ship was not very pleasant at all! Neither were the punishments pirates faced when they were captured. Around the world, authorities put captured pirates to death for their crimes. The bodies of executed pirates used to be placed in iron cages and hung from wooden frames where they could be easily seen. This was done to discourage others from becoming pirates. Although pirates still exist today, the Golden Age of piracy has sailed away.
pages.brief: A captured pirate faces execution by authorities, and his body is placed in an iron cage hanging from a wooden frame where people can see it. The grim scene warns others away from piracy. In the distance, a pirate ship sails off as the Golden Age of piracy passes.
