books.title: The Inuit: Northern Living
books.art_why: The book shows real Arctic landscapes, animals, Inuit people, homes, tools, and modern communities that can be photographed.

pages.text: Arctic Circle The Frozen North There is a place on Earth where it is always cold. The ground is frozen and the land is flat. For much of the year, it is covered in a white blanket of snow. This land is so far north that during the winter, the sun doesn’t come above the horizon. The land remains dark twenty-four hours a day. But during the summer, the Sun is always above the horizon. It is light outside twenty-four hours a day. That’s why this place, the Arctic, is sometimes called the “Land of the Midnight Sun.” If you visit the Arctic region, you’ll feel how cold it is. The temperature on an average winter day is about –34° Celsius (–30°F)! Each year, between 38 and 229 centimeters (15–90 in.) of snow fall. For many months, the Arctic’s rivers, lakes, and seas freeze over.
pages.brief: A vast flat Arctic landscape under a white blanket of snow, showing winter darkness with no sun above the horizon, then summer light with the sun low over frozen rivers, lakes, and sea; icy ground stretches to the horizon, conveying extreme cold and the midnight sun.

pages.text: So if it’s that cold and snowy, how can anything survive in the Arctic? The land is mostly barren tundra where even trees cannot grow. But some plants can take root in the far north. These are low-growing mosses, shrubs, and tiny flowering plants. Animals have also found ways to live in the Arctic. Salmon, lake trout, and Arctic cod are fish that swim in the cold waters. Whales, seals, walruses, and polar bears live in and around the sea. Layers of fat beneath their skin serve as warm insulation. Wolves, foxes, and caribou roam the tundra. Their thick coats of fur help keep them warm. In the summertime, ducks and geese migrate to the Arctic to build nests and raise their young. Caribou are a type of wild reindeer that live in North America.
pages.brief: On barren tundra, low mosses, shrubs, and tiny flowering plants grow; nearby cold water holds salmon, lake trout, and Arctic cod while whales, seals, walruses, and polar bears live in and around the sea. Wolves, foxes, and caribou roam the flat land, and ducks and geese tend nests with young in summer.

pages.text: So if plants and animals can survive in the far north, what about people? How would you stay warm during the cold, dark winters? How would you stay protected from the icy winds and snowstorms? How would you find food? People have lived in and near the Arctic for thousands of years. They could teach you a lot about surviving in the Arctic! An Inuit woman stays warm in her fur-lined parka.
pages.brief: An Inuit woman stands outdoors in cold, windy Arctic conditions, warmly dressed in a thick fur-lined parka with a hood; icy wind and snow swirl around her as she stays protected, showing how people survive the far north.

pages.text: The Inuit are a group of Indigenous people who live in the Arctic regions of North America. One region of their land is called Nunavut (NOO-nah-voot), which means “our land” in Inuktitut (ee-NOOK-tee-toot), the Inuit native language. Inuit ancestors lived in North America long before Europeans came to the Americas. Over time, the Inuit spread out to live in many different areas. Some of them lived just south of the Arctic where there are trees. There, houses are more easily made of wood. But in the far north, the Inuit use whale bones, hides, earth, and snow to build their homes. A Name for Ourselves You may have heard the Inuit referred to as “Eskimos.” This name is largely considered unacceptable by the Inuit. “Eskimo” was assigned to the Inuit by non-Indigenous people. Most Inuit prefer to be called by names they give themselves, in their own language. Some examples of these names are Inupiaq and Yupik.
pages.brief: Inuit families across Arctic North America, including Nunavut, are shown in their homeland; some live near trees where wooden houses stand, while others in the far north build homes from whale bones, hides, earth, and snow. Inuit people appear in traditional clothing within their communities.

pages.text: Staying Warm The Inuit know how to stay warm in freezing conditions. For centuries, they have used the skins of Arctic animals to make clothing suitable for the Arctic weather. They sew these skins into pants, socks, boots, and gloves. The most important article of clothing is the parka, which is a thick, hooded jacket. Because the clothes are handmade, they can be sized to perfectly fit the person. Caribou skin is a popular material because it is lightweight, yet warm. The Inuit have also used skins from foxes, seals, and polar bears. They decorate their clothing with beads and carvings. Some Inuit use innovative goggles to protect their eyes from “snow blindness,” or eye damage from the harsh sunlight reflecting off the white snow and ice. Historically, they carved these goggles out of wood and bone. A small slit in the material allowed the person to see while protecting their eyes. These goggles worked like sunglasses. These days, sunglasses are more widely available and used.
pages.brief: Inuit people sew animal skins into pants, socks, boots, gloves, and thick hooded parkas, decorated with beads and carvings. One person wears carved wooden or bone snow goggles with a narrow slit to protect eyes from bright snow and ice; caribou, fox, seal, and polar bear skins are nearby.

pages.text: Inside an igloo, an Inuit elder demonstrates use of a traditional toy. Inuit houses have always been an important part of staying warm. Traditional Inuit houses are built from a variety of materials, including driftwood, rocks, and sod. Caribou skins help to insulate the walls. Oil lamps heat and light these homes. This oil can come from melted animal fat, usually from seals, walruses, or whales. The lamps’ wicks were traditionally made of moss and grass. During long and snowy winters when other materials were scarce, the Inuit historically made houses out of snow and ice. These houses are warm and well insulated against the cold. They are tall enough for adults to stand up in, and often have side rooms for storage. Sometimes these houses have underground passages connecting them to neighboring houses so people can move around without having to face the Arctic winter.
pages.brief: Inside a warm Inuit home, an elder shows a traditional toy; walls are lined with caribou skins, and a moss-and-grass wick burns in an oil lamp. Nearby, a snow-and-ice house has storage side rooms and an underground passage connecting to a neighboring home.

pages.text: Today, a wider range of building materials are available in remote Arctic regions, but some hunters still use igloos. In Inuktitut, “igloo” means “house.” Igloos are also still useful for people seeking emergency shelter from the cold. The weather outside is so cold that igloos do not melt in the winter, and sometimes not even in the summer. But on the inside, igloos can be quite warm. Long entrance tunnels (just big enough to crawl through) keep out the wind and the cold. Historically, oil lamps, cooking fires, and body heat warmed up the main room. Adults and kids slept on platforms made of snow and covered with animal skin. Some igloos had windows made from clear lake ice. Caribou or seal skins lined the inside walls and kept the snow and ice from melting by trapping the heat inside. This Inuit man cuts out blocks of hard snow with a long knife. He will stack the blocks in a circle that spirals to close at the top.
pages.brief: An Inuit man cuts hard snow blocks with a long knife and stacks them in a circle that spirals closed at the top. The finished igloo has a long crawl-in entrance tunnel, snow sleeping platforms covered with animal skins, and a window made from clear lake ice.

pages.text: Venturing Out for Food The Inuit have trained dogs to pull sleds over the snow. In winter, this is a fast and reliable form of transportation. The sleds rest on skis made from whalebones. Some people still use teams of sled dogs today, but snowmobiles are also used for transportation. In the summer, the Inuit walk over land to gather berries, seaweed, bird eggs, and wild vegetables. When winter ice thaws, the Inuit are able to travel by boat. A common boat for one or two people is called a kayak (KIE-yak). Kayaks are narrow boats with covered tops. Paddlers sit down into small openings. Historically, the Inuit sealed the openings around themselves to prevent water from getting inside. Good kayaks are so well balanced that if they tip, paddlers can easily roll over until they are right side up again. Today, some Inuit use boats with motors as well.
pages.brief: A team of trained dogs pulls a sled over snow, with whalebone skis beneath it, while a snowmobile stands nearby. In summer, Inuit people walk the land gathering berries, seaweed, bird eggs, and wild vegetables; a paddler sits in a narrow covered kayak sealed around the opening on cold water.

pages.text: The frozen tundra ground is not good for growing crops. Historically, there were no stores to buy goods from, so the Inuit traveled by sled, boat, and foot to hunt, fish, and harvest plants.
pages.brief: On frozen tundra where crops cannot grow, Inuit people travel by dog sled, boat, and on foot to hunt, fish, and harvest plants. With no stores nearby, they carry food and goods across the snow and open water, working across the wide, treeless Arctic landscape.

pages.text: Even though non-native vegetables, fruits, and milk are sometimes available in the Arctic, there may be long shipping times and high prices. That often means food is not fresh but still costs a lot of money. For this reason, harvesting native plants is still common. The Inuit also hunt for food. But like many Indigenous communities, they have great respect for the land. Because of this respect, the Inuit make full use of the animals they harvest. For example, whales are harvested for food. However, the Inuit also melt whale fat into oil, which heats and lights homes. Whale bones are used to make knives and tools, like snow goggles. An Inuit hunter wears pants and boots made from polar bear fur as he checks his hunting trap.
pages.brief: An Inuit hunter in pants and boots made from polar bear fur checks a hunting trap on the snowy land. Nearby, whale fat is melted into oil for heat and light, whale bones become knives and tools, and native plants are gathered; imported food sits costly and less fresh.

pages.text: Work and Play Traditionally, Inuit men spent much of their time hunting, fishing, and making tools. Women often cooked, skinned animals, and sewed skins into clothing. The kids helped out with these chores until they were old enough to do them alone. Before colonization, Inuit children didn’t attend school inside at desks all day. Education was more community-based. Traditional Inuit Education Lesson Educator Compares To listening to stories, participating in community ceremonies and institutions social studies, history, public speaking elders, community members preparing pelts and skins for making clothing, cooking and food prep, sewing, wood chopping older women in the extended family home economics navigating, fishing, and hunting older men in the extended family geography, life skills.
pages.brief: In a traditional Inuit camp, men hunt, fish, and make tools while women cook, skin animals, and sew skins into clothing. Children help with chores, learning by watching and working alongside elders and family members rather than sitting at desks in a classroom.

pages.text: Harsh Arctic winters can keep Inuit families inside for days at a time. Stories, songs, and play are important tools people use to build community when the going gets tough. Computers and phones help isolated communities stay connected through long winter months. Historically, kids played with dolls, bows and arrows, and leather balls. They also decorated pins, combs, and goggles with carvings that looked like animals. Fathers often made “story knives” for their daughters. Girls used these story knives to draw pictures on the ground or in the snow. Friends try to guess the artist’s subject or the story being told. Today, girls still play this game, often swapping out the traditional knives made of bone or wood for metal butter knives. One tradition-turned-game is called nalukataq, or “blanket toss.” A person stands on a large blanket made of skins, and many people gather around the blanket and pull it tight to launch the person into the air. This was originally a way for hunters to scout terrain. Now, they can use binoculars for that, but the blanket toss has become a game. The goal is to land on your feet after every toss. Some people even do flips!
pages.brief: Inside during a long winter, Inuit families tell stories, sing, and play; children use dolls, bows and arrows, and leather balls, and girls draw pictures in snow with story knives while friends guess the tale. Outside, people pull a skin blanket tight to toss a person high into the air.

pages.text: The Inuit Today Before the arrival of Qallunaat (kah-loo- NAHT) (people who are not Inuit, typically white people), the Inuit used their vast knowledge of animal migration patterns, plant life, and the patterns of the sea to thrive. When Europeans arrived, foreign fur trappers and miners tricked the Inuit into accepting very low prices for their furs. The European traders sold furs for high prices in Europe but paid the Inuit in low-cost traded goods like flour and tea. Foreign governments have also divided Inuit land into countries, provinces, and territories. They have separated Inuit communities and made it difficult to practice traditional ways of life. Because of colonization, many Inuit have been forced to find jobs outside their communities. Children can no longer be taught primarily by their elders and community. They instead leave home to go to school in classrooms. Because of this, traditional practices and languages are threatened, though the Inuit work hard to protect their culture. Since the 1970s, governments have worked to ensure Inuit children learn the Inuktitut language in school.
pages.brief: Inuit families face changes brought by colonization: foreign traders exchange flour and tea for furs, governments divide Inuit land, and children leave home for classroom schools. Inuit people work to protect their culture and Inuktitut language, while some must find jobs outside their communities.

pages.text: The patterns of animal movements have also been greatly affected by colonialism and the growth of industry. New people and businesses moving into the area have caused changes. Oil pipelines interfere with caribou migration. Invasive species of fish are now often found in Arctic waterways. Human-caused climate change has also affected weather patterns. Snowfalls are heavier, ice comes for a shorter time, and is not as thick or reliable as it once was. These lasting effects of colonialism create challenges for the Inuit. Climate change is responsible for unusual amounts of melting ice in the Arctic and other cold areas around the world. Traditional Inuit Lands Russia Greenland Alaska Arctic Circle Canada United States Today over 100,000 Inuit live in parts of four different countries.
pages.brief: Across the Arctic, oil pipelines cut across caribou migration routes, invasive fish swim in waterways, and melting ice shows climate change. Inuit communities spread across Russia, Greenland, Alaska, Canada, and the United States continue to live with these changes to snow, ice, and animal movement.

pages.text: Conclusion If you visited the far north today, you would need to bundle up. If you went in the wintertime, it would be dark in the middle of the day. It would be freezing cold for days and weeks and months. A visit to the Arctic might make you wish you knew as much as your Inuit peers about how to thrive in this harsh environment! Just beyond the city of Anchorage, Alaska, the frozen Chugach Mountains stand tall.
pages.brief: Beyond Anchorage, Alaska, the tall frozen Chugach Mountains stand under cold sky. A visitor bundled in winter clothing looks out over the icy northern landscape, imagining the dark midday winter and learning from Inuit peers how to thrive in the harsh environment.

pages.text: Explore More 1 At the Library Ask your librarian where you can find books about the Inuit and the Arctic. 2 On the Web A. Type Inuit into a search engine. B. Read through the search results. Click on a link that looks interesting. C. Try some different searches: Inuktitut, Arctic, Nunavut, tundra. 3 Try This! Wherever we come from, our behaviors and practices change over time, often as a result of our environments, or our stage of life. Try talking to an elder in your life. This could be a family member or someone else you know. Ask them about something they used to do that they no longer do. Or ask about something they have started doing recently! Have a conversation about how life changes because of your age, environment, and big events. You might hear a story you have never heard before!
pages.brief: An elder and a younger person sit together in a warm home, talking and sharing a story. A library shelf and a computer nearby suggest looking for books and searching for more information about the Inuit, Inuktitut, Nunavut, the Arctic, and the tundra.

books.title: The Amazing Amazon
books.art_why: The Amazon rainforest, its animals, river, and plants are real places and living things today.

pages.text: Chapter 1: There Is a Place There is a place where monkeys swing and howl, jaguars leap from tree to tree, bananas and pineapples grow for free, tiny frogs live in flowers, and pink-colored dolphins swim in the river. This is where storms come often, and where the air is sweet. Some sunlight filters through the vines and leaves, but it is mostly dark here on the ground. It is hot, steamy, and surprisingly still, except for the rainwater that trickles down from leaf to leaf. You hear a slow sound: drip, drip, drip. Your skin is sweaty, an insect lands on your neck, and an ant quietly walks across your sandal. Suddenly a little brown monkey swings to a nearby branch, and then a bright green bird flutters past. Welcome to the Amazon rainforest.
pages.brief: An Amazon rainforest scene: monkeys swing and howl, a jaguar leaps between trees, bananas and pineapples grow, a tiny frog sits in a flower, and pink dolphins swim in the river. Rain trickles from leaf to leaf. A monkey swings nearby, a bright green bird flutters past, an insect lands on a visitor’s neck, and an ant crosses a sandal.

pages.text: Rainforests Tropical rainforests live up to their name: They are forests where it rains a lot. In fact, a typical tropical rainforest receives between 150 and 400 centimeters (59–157 in) of rain each year. They are also warm. Their temperature averages between 25° and 35° Celsius (77°F–95°F). Rainforests are green year-round. Their hot, humid, and rainy climate is perfect for tall trees, vines, ferns, and other plants. The really thick parts of rainforests are what we call jungle. Tropical rainforests cover a small part (about 6 percent) of Earth’s surface, but over half (50 percent) of the world’s plant and animal species are found in them! Rainforests usually lie in tropical areas near Earth’s equator. Most of the world’s rainforests are in Africa, Southeast Asia, and South America.
pages.brief: A lush tropical rainforest receives heavy rain and warm temperatures, staying green all year. Tall trees, vines, ferns, and other plants grow thickly, forming jungle. Many kinds of plants and animals live among the trees. This rainforest lies near Earth’s equator, with most rainforests found in Africa, Southeast Asia, and South America.

pages.text: The Amazon The Amazon rainforest lies in South America. It is the largest tropical rainforest in the world, and it has more kinds of insects, plants, and animals than any other place on Earth. Every year, scientists discover new species of insects and plants here. The Amazon River flows through the heart of this rainforest. It is like a huge sea of fresh water. Thousands of other rivers and streams empty into it. Catfish, piranhas, and dolphins all live in the Amazon River. This book will take you on a tour of the Amazon rainforest. You will travel from the tallest trees to the rainforest floor. Along the way, you will meet an eagle, monkey, jaguar, and ant. You will even hear what these Amazon natives would say—if they could talk.
pages.brief: The Amazon rainforest in South America is the world’s largest rainforest, with many insects, plants, and animals. The Amazon River flows through its heart like a sea of fresh water, with thousands of streams emptying into it. Catfish, piranhas, and dolphins swim there. An eagle, monkey, jaguar, and ant appear on a tour from tall trees to the forest floor.

pages.text: Map of Amazon Basin ATLANTIC OCEAN The Amazon River So just how big is the Amazon River? • The Amazon River can be more than 48 kilometers (30 mi) across at its widest point during the rainy season. • It flows almost 6,437 kilometers (4,000 mi) to the Atlantic Ocean. • Within its mouth is an island the size of Switzerland. • The river’s arapaima fish can grow to be 3 meters (10 ft) long and weigh 180 kilograms (400 lb)! • Its volume of water is greater than the next eight largest rivers combined! The Amazon is the world’s widest and largest river.
pages.brief: A broad view of the Amazon Basin shows the wide Amazon River winding through rainforest toward the Atlantic Ocean. During the rainy season the river can stretch more than 48 kilometers across. A large island sits within its mouth, and a huge arapaima fish swims in the water. Its water volume is greater than the next eight largest rivers combined.

pages.text: From the Amazon Yearbook Sloths are slow- moving animals. They seem to just hang out (upside down!) in the trees. Sloths get covered in algae, which helps them blend into the forest. Sammy was voted: Most Likely to Survive, but Least Likely to Succeed Sammy “Slowpoke” Sloth The tapir is a big, hoofed animal that is related to the horse and the rhinoceros. Tapirs often weigh well over 136 kilograms (300 lb). Tapirs like to take baths in the river and look for food when it is dark. Tamara the Tapir Tamara was voted: Best Personality.
pages.brief: Sammy “Slowpoke” Sloth hangs upside down in a tree, slow-moving and covered in algae that helps him blend into the forest. Tamara the Tapir, a big hoofed animal related to horses and rhinoceroses, takes a bath in the river and looks for food in the dark. Both animals appear in a playful yearbook-style portrait.

pages.text: From the Amazon Yearbook At around 1.2 meters (4 ft) long, the capybara is the world’s largest rodent. (But Katie doesn’t like to be called a big rat.) Capybaras’ webbed feet help them swim. Katie was voted: Most Likely to Win a Rat Race The poison arrow frog has super-bright colors that warn other animals that its skin is poisonous. Indians in the Amazon rainforest dip their arrows into this poison for hunting. Paulo was voted: Most Dangerous Amphibian.
pages.brief: Katie the Capybara, the world’s largest rodent, swims with webbed feet and measures about 1.2 meters long. Paulo the Poison Arrow Frog shows super-bright colors that warn other animals his skin is poisonous. An Indigenous hunter in the Amazon dips an arrow into the frog’s poison for hunting. The two animals appear in playful yearbook-style portraits.

pages.text: Chapter 2: Layers of the Rainforest To better understand the rainforest, scientists have “divided” it into four layers, or sections. You can think of it like a four-story building. The highest trees make up the top floor, or the emergent layer; the next-highest trees make up the canopy layer; below them is the understory layer; and at the bottom is the rainforest floor. Rainforest Layers Emergent Layer Canopy Layer Understory Layer Rainforest Floor.
pages.brief: A tall rainforest shown as four stacked levels, like a four-story building. The highest trees form the top level, the emergent layer. Below them, the next-highest trees make the canopy layer. Under that is the understory, and at the bottom lies the rainforest floor. Each level is filled with branches, leaves, and vines.

pages.text: High Risers The tallest trees of the rainforest are called the emergents. They resemble big umbrellas that rise high above the thick forest. Emergents are exposed to lots of sun, wind, rain, and lightning. Big roots support these giant trees. Because rainforest soil is shallow, tree roots often grow above the ground. The kapok tree, for example, has roots that extend out like wooden walls. These roots are so big that your whole class could hide behind just one of them! Not many animals live in the emergent layer. Some birds and butterflies do visit to eat leaves and fruit. One huge bird, the harpy eagle, actually lives up there, high above the Amazon. The harpy eagle has a very long wingspan when it fully extends its wings.
pages.brief: Giant emergent trees rise high above the rainforest like umbrellas, exposed to sun, wind, rain, and lightning. The kapok tree’s huge roots spread out above the shallow soil like wooden walls, big enough for a whole class to hide behind. A harpy eagle lives high up, wings fully extended. Birds and butterflies visit to eat leaves and fruit.

pages.text: Spotlight Interview: The Harpy Eagle Interviewer: Hello there, Harpy. Is it true that you are the largest eagle in the Americas? Harpy: I think so. In your people terms, I am about one meter tall, which is over three feet high. Interviewer: It looks like you have some big wings as well. Harpy: Oh, these things? I was born with these. If I stretch them out like this, they are longer than most people. You see? My wingspan is two meters across, which is about six and a half feet. Flying fast really helps me find food. Interviewer: What is your favorite food? Harpy: Oh, I like pizza delivered to my door. Just kidding—there’s no pizza here in the rainforest! I hunt sloths, monkeys, and fellow birds. Monkeys are probably the tastiest. Interviewer: Is that what your big talons are for? Harpy: Yep, these meat hooks can scoop unsuspecting animals right off of tree branches. Interviewer: Do you ever fear revenge, like a monkey uprising? Harpy: No, I’m the top bird around here. I build my stick nests in the tallest trees where monkeys don’t normally go. Hey, there’s a monkey now! I’ll see you later!
pages.brief: A large harpy eagle perches high in a tall Amazon tree, wings spread wide during an interview. The eagle is about one meter tall, with a two-meter wingspan and big talons. It says it hunts sloths, monkeys, and other birds, and builds stick nests in the tallest trees. A monkey appears nearby in the branches.

pages.text: Crazy Canopy The rainforest’s real action is in the canopy layer, because this is where most plants and animals live. It is like a thick roof woven out of tree branches, plants, and vines. Many trees in the canopy are covered with climbing vines and epiphytes, which are plants that grow on top of others. Most of the rainforest’s flowers, fruit, and seeds are found in this layer. With so much good canopy food, it makes sense that animals hang out here. Many animals rarely come down to the ground. They eat, sleep, hunt, and give birth high up in the trees. Sloths, toucans, and parrots are just some of the canopy’s residents. The hardest one to ignore is probably the howler monkey. Its name befits its behavior, as these monkeys howl and scream to keep other animals out of their territories. Bromeliads are cone- shaped plants that grow on trees. Their cones catch a lot of rainwater and form little swimming pools high above the ground, where tiny frogs, salamanders, and crabs live, and mosquitoes and dragonflies lay their eggs.
pages.brief: The thick canopy is a busy roof of branches, plants, and vines. Sloths, toucans, parrots, and a loud howler monkey live high up, eating, sleeping, hunting, and giving birth in the trees. Bromeliads, cone-shaped plants growing on branches, catch rainwater in little pools where tiny frogs, salamanders, crabs, mosquitoes, and dragonflies live or lay eggs.

pages.text: Spotlight Interview: The Howler Monkey Interviewer: Wow, that was one loud howl! Excuse me, but could you please stop screaming for one moment? I would like to ask you a few questions! Howler: Okay, but hurry up. If I don’t scream like this, other monkeys may come into our territory. Interviewer: Do you always stay up here in the canopy? Howler: This is our home, my man. On the ground, there are some really big animals—it’s a jungle down there. When it comes to safety, we don’t monkey around. Up here, we can eat fruit, leaves, and flowers, and we can live in safety. Interviewer: Does your long tail help you? It looks prehensile. Reaching the Top Scientists have found creative ways to study the top layers of rainforests. They have climbed with ropes and ladders, built platforms like tree houses, and gone up in cranes. A blimp has even lowered a raft of scientists down to the canopy.
pages.brief: A howler monkey clings to a canopy branch, howling loudly during an interview. Nearby, scientists reach the treetops by climbing with ropes and ladders, building platforms like tree houses, using a crane, and lowering a raft from a blimp. The monkey says it stays high for safety and eats fruit, leaves, and flowers.

pages.text: Howler: Yeah, if by prehensile you mean “grab onto.” My tail helps me climb, but my hands and feet are very useful for climbing, too. Interviewer: You sure use big words for a monkey. Hey, stop the howling! If you can be heard from miles away, just think how loud it is for me. What makes you so loud anyway? Howler: I have a special bone in my windpipe. My throat is like a hollow sound box. See the big swelling under my chin? Here, touch it. Interviewer: Oww, that’s not funny—you have sharp teeth! Okay, Mr. Monkey, you can go back to howling now.
pages.brief: The howler monkey grips a branch with its long prehensile tail and uses its hands and feet to climb. A close view shows the big swelling under its chin and its sharp teeth. The monkey explains that a special bone in its windpipe and a hollow, sound-box throat make its loud howl possible. The interviewer stands nearby.

pages.text: The Darker Story The understory is the third level of the rainforest. It is below the canopy and above the ground. This is where ferns, plants, and young trees grow. It is dark in the understory because very little light shines through the thick canopy. Understory plants grow leaves that are big and wide. That way, they have a better chance of catching some rays. Animals like to eat these big leaves. The understory is not nearly as busy as the canopy, but animals do live here. Poison arrow frogs hide in the foliage, snakes wrap around trees like vines, birds peck and pull insects from the wood, and large cats such as jaguars leap between branches.
pages.brief: The dark understory lies below the canopy and above the ground, where ferns, plants, and young trees grow. Their big, wide leaves reach for the little light that shines through. A poison arrow frog hides in the foliage, a snake wraps around a tree like a vine, a bird pecks insects from wood, and a jaguar leaps between branches.

pages.text: Spotlight Interview: The Jaguar Interviewer: Hey, put me down and don’t bite me! Bad cat, bad big cat! Jaguar: Sorry, I thought you were a monkey. Lucky you’re not as tasty. Hey, what do you think you’re doing here anyway? Interviewer: I came to interview you, the biggest cat in the Americas. Mr. Jaguar, are you really 2.6 meters (8.5 ft) long? Jaguar: That’s what they say. And I weigh 136 kilograms (300 lb), too. Not many animals mess with me. By the way, you can just call me Jag. Interviewer: Okay, Jag, what do you do for exercise? Jag: I get bored with just one sport. That’s why I cross-train: I run, swim, climb, fish, and hunt. Interviewer: What do you hunt? Jag: Lots of things. Sometimes I climb up in the canopy to eat sloths and monkeys. On the ground, I hunt peccaries, tapirs, and yummy capybaras. On lazy days, I lie near the river and catch fish with my claws. When I’m really hungry, I kill caimans. Interviewer: Wow, I don’t want to be in your powerful jaws ever again! If you’ll excuse me, I need to go now.
pages.brief: A jaguar speaks with an interviewer while resting near branches and a river. The big cat is 2.6 meters long and weighs 136 kilograms. It runs, swims, climbs, fishes, and hunts. It climbs into the canopy for sloths and monkeys, hunts peccaries, tapirs, and capybaras on the ground, catches fish with its claws, and kills caimans when very hungry.

pages.text: Chapter 3: Keeping It Clean If you walked around the rainforest floor, you might be surprised. It is not just one thick jungle. Sure, you would see roots, ferns, herbs, and baby trees, but most of the green would be high above you. Earthworms, termites, fungi, and bacteria eat up the fallen fruit, leaves, and branches. They recycle it back into nutritious soil. When a big tree falls, they quickly munch it down into small pieces. Also on the ground are big animals like deer, tapirs, peccaries, and capybaras, but they are far outnumbered by the smaller spiders, beetles, and ants. Ant highways crisscross the rainforest floor. One kind of ant even parades around with leaves and flower petals in its mouth. It is the famous leaf-cutter ant. The rainforest floor is covered in branches, ferns, and fallen leaves. Trivia Question In the Amazon rainforest, are there more mammals, birds, insects, or reptiles? Answer: Insects! (There are more than two hundred types of mosquitoes alone. There are well over one thousand different kinds of butterflies. And just think of all the ants!)
pages.brief: The rainforest floor is covered with branches, ferns, fallen leaves, and baby trees. Earthworms, termites, fungi, and bacteria eat fallen fruit, leaves, and branches, recycling them into soil. Deer, tapirs, peccaries, and capybaras live here, but spiders, beetles, and ants are far more numerous. Leaf-cutter ants parade with leaves and flower petals, while many insects and butterflies fill the rainforest.

pages.text: Spotlight Interview: The Leaf-Cutter Ant Interviewer: Hey down there! Yeah, you—the one carrying the big leaf over your head! I’d like to ask you a few questions. Do you have a moment? Ms. Ant: Sure, but I do need to hurry back to the fungus garden because we’re low on food. Interviewer: Did you really just climb up a tree and cut off that leaf? Ms. Ant: That’s correct. And now I’m carrying it back to our underground colony, where smaller ants will chew it up into little spongy bits. Interviewer: So you don’t eat the actual leaf? Ms. Ant: No, we use the leaves to grow fungus. Then we eat the fungus. Want to try some? Interviewer: No, thank you—I, uh, just had lunch. So tell me, what is it like underground? Ms. Ant: We have deep nests with hundreds of chambers. In the middle rooms, small ants tend to our fungus gardens. Our only queen is in a different room. She can lay up to thirty thousand eggs in one day. That’s why there are almost five million of us here! Now if you’ll excuse me, I need to sniff my way home. And please watch your feet—if you step on our trail, I might get lost!
pages.brief: Ms. Ant carries a big leaf over her head toward an underground colony while an interviewer watches. Inside the deep nest are hundreds of chambers, including rooms where smaller ants chew leaves into spongy bits and tend fungus gardens. A queen in another room can lay up to thirty thousand eggs in one day. Almost five million ants live there.

pages.text: Chapter 4: Who, Me? Yes, you. Do you eat bananas? Do you like chocolate? Have you ridden a bicycle with rubber tires? Well, guess what! Bananas, chocolate, and rubber all grow in the Amazon rainforest. Many more things come from the Amazon, too, such as medicines, wood, pineapples, and fresh air.
pages.brief: A child rides a bicycle with rubber tires beside bananas, chocolate, medicines, wood, and pineapples, all from the Amazon. Green plants around them also make fresh air. The scene links everyday things—bananas, chocolate, rubber tires—to the rainforest.

pages.text: The Amazon is a rich, living treasure. Insects buzz by that do not even have names yet. Trees grow, fall, and turn back into soil. Rainstorms fill up frogs’ swimming pools. And perhaps most importantly, plants of the rainforest take carbon dioxide from the air and replace it with oxygen. Humans and other animals need oxygen in order to live. The Amazon rainforest is a real place. Even if it is far away from you, the Amazon lives at this very moment. As you read these words, a jaguar slinks through the understory. Right now, a leaf-cutter ant marches back to a fungus garden. Somewhere in the Amazon, the scream of a howler monkey echoes throughout the forest. Can you hear it?
pages.brief: The Amazon is a living treasure. Unnamed insects buzz, trees grow and fall back into soil, and rainstorms fill frogs’ swimming pools. Green plants take carbon dioxide from the air and replace it with oxygen. A jaguar slinks through the understory, a leaf-cutter ant marches to a fungus garden, and a howler monkey’s scream echoes through the forest.

pages.text: Explore More Did you like learning about the Amazon rainforest? Well, there is much more to see. If you do some research, you’re bound to find some very interesting animals! 1. At the Library Tell your librarian that you are interested in books about the Amazon rainforest. 2. On the Web In the address window, type: www.google.com Then type: Amazon rainforest. Click on “Google Search.” Read the colored links. Click on one that looks interesting. When you want to explore other links, click the “back” arrow on the top left. Or try a new search: Amazon River.
pages.brief: A child visits a library and speaks with a librarian about books on the Amazon rainforest. Nearby, a computer is open for a search about the Amazon rainforest, then a search about the Amazon River. The child explores library shelves and online links to learn more about the rainforest.

pages.text: 3. Try This! Where do you live? Do you live in the rainforest? What about in a desert, tundra, or pine forest? Do you live on the coast, up in the mountains, or out on the plains? You must live somewhere, right? If you live in a town or city, sometimes it can be hard to tell what kind of region you live in. But there are clues all around. What kinds of trees and bushes grow nearby? What kinds of birds fly overhead? What is the weather like? Look around and investigate. If you are not sure, ask your teacher, librarian, parent, or friend. Once you figure it out, make a report. Draw a picture like the one on page 10, but make it for your area. What kind of insects, plants, and animals are native to your home? You could find this information by walking around outside. You could also ask other people. Or you could read a book, or search the Web. You’ll probably be surprised by the cool things you learn about your neighbors!
pages.brief: A child investigates their own area, looking at nearby trees, bushes, birds, and weather. They draw a picture report of local insects, plants, and animals, and ask a teacher, librarian, parent, or friend for help. Books and a computer sit nearby for research. The child looks around outside to discover what kinds of living things are neighbors.

books.title: The Hard Stuff! All About Bones
books.art_why: Real bones, skeletons and people can be shown with photographs.

pages.text: The Hard Stuff! All About Bones.
pages.brief: A human skeleton stands against a plain background, with bones of the skull, rib cage, arms and legs clearly visible, introducing a book about bones. Its hard bones show the frame that supports a body and helps it move.

pages.text: Body Shapers Lizards have one. Elephants have one. Even fish have one. You have one, too! What do you all have? You all have skeletons. Skeletons are the bones inside animals’ bodies. The skeleton is a frame that has muscles, blood vessels, and skin wrapped around it. Skeletons give vertebrates —humans and many other animals—their shape. You can identify many animals just by looking at their skeletons.
pages.brief: A lion, cow, seal, elephant, monkey, lizard, fish and human are shown together, each with its skeleton visible inside or beside its body, showing that vertebrates have skeletons that give them shape. You can identify many animals just by looking at their skeletons.

pages.text: The human skeleton is made up of 206 bones, starting at the top with the skull and ending at the bottom with the toe bones. Many bones have muscles attached to them by tendons. These bones help us move. Some bones protect soft organs inside our bodies, such as the heart and the brain. Many large bones have special areas in the center that make blood cells. Tissues called ligaments connect the bones to make up the skeleton. To learn how bones work, let’s take a closer look at specific body areas. ligaments Ligaments hold the hand and foot bones together.
pages.brief: A complete human skeleton stands from skull to toe bones, with muscles attached by tendons and ligaments holding hand and foot bones together; the heart and brain are shown inside protective bony areas. The skeleton shows the body's frame.

pages.text: These bike riders wear helmets to protect their skulls. Heads Up Think about the human forehead—the part of the face above the eyebrows. Do you think it is soft, like a pillow, or hard, like a desk? The forehead is hard because the skull, or cranium, is right there under the skin. The cranium is one set of bones in the body. It protects the brain, a very important and very soft organ. The cranium is like a crash helmet, except that it is not as strong. For that reason, people need to wear helmets when they play some sports.
pages.brief: Bike riders wear helmets while riding, showing head protection. A close view of a person’s forehead and skull shows the hard cranium beneath the skin, with the soft brain protected inside, like a crash helmet for sports.

pages.text: If you think about your head, your skull might seem to be one piece. Actually, though, the skull is made up of many different bones. The bones come together at special joints called sutures. Unlike other joints, sutures don’t move much. Remember the forehead? This part of the skull is the frontal bone. The ridge of bone above your eyes is the supraorbital ridge. The largest part of your skull covers the top and back of the head. These two bones are the parietal (puh-RY-eh-tul) bones. The part of the skull just above the neck in the back is the occipital (awk-SIP-ih-tul) bone, and the sides of the skull, above the ears, are the temporal bones. Major Skull Bones frontal bone parietal bone supraorbital ridge sutures occipital bone temporal bone.
pages.brief: A human skull is shown with the forehead, the ridge above the eyes, the top and back, the lower back above the neck, and the sides above the ears visible as separate skull bones. These bones meet at fixed joints called sutures and do not move much.

pages.text: In all, the skull has twenty-two bones, not counting the six in the middle ears and one in the throat. Under the cheeks, it is possible to feel the cheekbones, or zygomatic bones. The jaw is made up of two bones— the upper jaw, or maxilla, and the lower jaw, or mandible. The lower jaw is one of the few bones in the skull that can move on its own. cheekbone upper jaw bone lower jaw bone Bones Bonus The ears also have bones—the hammer, anvil, and stirrup, which are attached to the eardrum. These bones are the tiniest bones in your body. When the eardrum picks up sounds and vibrates, the eardrum moves the hammer. The hammer then vibrates, which makes the anvil vibrate, which in turn pushes the stirrup. Nerves detect these vibrations and send them to the brain, which makes meaning of the sounds. For those who are deaf or hard of hearing, hearing aids act as an amplifier. Hearing aids help the brain better pick up the vibrations from the hammer.
pages.brief: A human skull shows the cheekbones and the upper and lower jaw, with the lower jaw able to move. Nearby, the tiny ear bones - hammer, anvil and stirrup - are shown attached to the eardrum, and a hearing aid helps amplify vibrations.

pages.text: Cartilage is softer than bones, but teeth are harder. If you look at a skeleton, you might see something missing from its face—a nose. The part of the nose that sticks out is not made of bone but rather of a tissue called cartilage (CAR-tih-ledj). A nose can be touched and moved around. Cartilage, unlike your bones, can bend. Cartilage, which is also found at the ends of bones, keeps them from rubbing together. Skeletons also have teeth, but teeth are not bones. Teeth are harder than bones. The outside of a tooth is made of a substance called enamel. Enamel is the hardest substance in the body.
pages.brief: A human face and skeleton show the nose made of bendable cartilage rather than bone, cartilage at the ends of bones, and teeth with hard enamel on the outside. The nose can be touched and moved.

pages.text: Put Your Back into It The skull connects to the backbone, also called the spinal column. The first few parts of the spinal column start at the back of the neck. The ridges of the spinal column continue down your back, all the way to your hips. These ridges, called vertebrae (VER-teh-bray), are the individual bones of the backbone. The backbone has thirty-three vertebrae. Seven vertebrae—the cervical vertebrae—are in the neck. Twelve vertebrae run from the top of the back to about the middle of the back. They are the thoracic (thor-AH-sik) vertebrae. Five lumbar vertebrae are at the back of the waist, followed by five fused sacral vertebrae, which sit between the hips. The remaining vertebrae form the coccyx (KOK-siks) at the bottom of the spinal column. The vertebrae in the neck allow people to look up high. Bones Bonus The top two vertebrae are the atlas and axis. These two vertebrae allow people to nod and shake their heads.
pages.brief: The skull connects to the spinal column, shown from the neck down to the hips. The vertebrae include cervical bones in the neck, thoracic bones in the upper back, lumbar bones at the waist, fused sacral bones between the hips, and the coccyx at the bottom. Top vertebrae allow nodding and shaking.

pages.text: Spinal Column cervical vertebrae thoracic vertebrae lumbar vertebrae sacrum coccyx Side View Front View The spinal column has two important jobs. First, it protects the soft spinal cord, which runs through the vertebrae. The spinal cord is the place where all the nerves in the body meet to send information to the brain. The spinal column also allows bodies to bend, twist, roll, and flip. Because the backbone is a chain of bones instead of one solid bone, it is very flexible and can move in many directions.
pages.brief: Side and front views of the spinal column show its vertebrae protecting the soft spinal cord inside. The chain of bones lets a body bend, twist, roll and flip, while nerves in the spinal cord carry information toward the brain.

pages.text: The skull is not the only set of bones attached to the backbone; the ribs and pelvic bones are attached to it, too. Along with giving shape to the chest, the ribs protect the lungs and heart. If a person bangs on their chest, their lungs and heart don’t get squashed because the ribs provide a sturdy wall around them. A rib cage has twelve bones on each side, each of which is connected to one of the twelve thoracic vertebrae. Front View Side View clavicle scapula ribs spinal column pelvis.
pages.brief: The rib cage, pelvic bones, collarbone and shoulder blade are shown attached to the spinal column. The ribs form a sturdy wall around the lungs and heart, with twelve rib bones on each side connected to thoracic vertebrae.

pages.text: Near the top end of the spinal column, you will also find a scapula and clavicle on each side. Scapula is the technical term for the shoulder blade, and clavicle is the technical term for the collarbone. The scapula and the clavicle make up the shoulder. Near the bottom of the spinal column, two hip bones form the pelvis. On each side, a pelvic bone looks like a shallow dish or bowl. That’s because it holds the intestines and other lower-body organs. Boning Up The skeleton of a newborn baby is not the same as the skeleton of an adult. Before birth, a body has cartilage instead of bones. As the body grows and develops, the cartilage hardens and turns to bone. By the time a baby is born, most of the cartilage has become bone. As babies become children and then adults, their bones continue to harden or even join together. One of the last sets of bones to join together is the group that makes up the pelvis. These bones become one solid structure when a person is in their late teens or early twenties. sacrum pelvic bones.
pages.brief: A shoulder shows the scapula and clavicle forming the shoulder, while two hip bones form the pelvis near the bottom of the spinal column. The pelvis holds the intestines and lower-body organs, and a newborn skeleton is shown with cartilage turning to bone. The pelvic bones become one solid structure in late teens or early twenties.

pages.text: And Now the Appendages Arms and hands, legs and feet—a body’s appendages — allow people to perform different activities. Arms and hands allow people to lift and hold things, while legs and feet help people move around. These actions are possible in part because of the bones inside the body’s appendages. humerus ulna radius Each arm contains three bones—the humerus, the radius, and the ulna. The humerus is the upper-arm bone, attached at the top to the shoulder. The radius and the ulna make up the lower part of the arm, between the elbow and wrist. wrist bones palm bones thumb and finger bones These kids use the ir arms to help hold themselves up.
pages.brief: Children use their arms to hold themselves up, showing how arms and hands lift and hold while legs and feet help people move. A skeleton of an arm shows the humerus, radius and ulna, with wrist, palm, thumb and finger bones visible.

pages.text: The wrist and hand together have more bones than any other part of the body—twenty-seven! That’s a total of fifty-four bones for both hands. Because wrists and hands have so many bones, they are very flexible and precise, allowing people to do complex activities such as tying shoelaces or writing. Many for Manipulating Fingers may be smaller than arms, but they have more bones. Here’s how the number of bones in each part of the arms and hands compare. Arm: 3 bones Wrist: 8 carpals Palm: 5 metacarpals Each finger: 3 phalanges (fuh-LAN-jeez) Each thumb: 2 phalanges Fingers and thumb: 14 phalanges total.
pages.brief: A hand and wrist are shown doing a precise task, such as tying shoelaces or writing, with many small bones making them flexible. The arm has three bones, the wrist eight, the palm five, and the fingers and thumb fourteen phalanges in all.

pages.text: The bones of the legs and feet are similar to the bones of the arms and hands. The top portion of the leg is one solid bone, called the thighbone, or femur. The bottom part of the leg has two bones—the shinbone, or tibia, and the fibula. Between the upper and lower parts of the leg is one more bone—the kneecap, or patella. The kneecap lies over the knee joint, protecting the tendons beneath it that allow the leg to bend. Bones Bonus The longest, strongest, and largest bone in the human body is in the leg. It’s the thighbone, or femur. The femur extends from the pelvis to the knee. To break the femur requires a large amount of force—for example, a person would have to fall from a great height or have a high- speed collision while skiing or skating.
pages.brief: A human leg shows the thighbone, or femur, as one solid upper bone, with the shinbone and fibula below and the kneecap over the knee joint. The kneecap protects the tendons beneath it that let the leg bend, and the femur is the longest and strongest bone.

pages.text: Like the hand, the foot is a complex collection of many bones. Each foot has one fewer bone than a hand—twenty-six—for a total of fifty-two bones for both feet. The ankle and heel of a foot have seven tarsal bones, and the ball of a foot has five metatarsal bones. Like the hand, the foot has fourteen phalanges —two for the big toe and three each for the remaining toes. Skin and tissue on the bottoms, or soles, of the feet protect the bones from the impact of jumping and running. Foot bones are cushioned by the skin and tissue around them so they don’t break when people run, jump, and hop. femur patella fibula tibia ankle bones ball toe bones.
pages.brief: A foot is shown with its many bones: seven tarsal bones in the ankle and heel, five metatarsal bones in the ball, and fourteen phalanges in the toes. Skin and tissue on the sole cushion the foot when a person runs, jumps and hops.

pages.text: Joints allow people to bend and twist into all kinds of positions. Don’t Get Out of Joint Along with 206 bones, the adult human body has over 100 joints. Joints are the places where bones meet. Bones are hard and unbending, but because bones are connected at joints, our bodies can bend and twist. Bones Bonus Sometimes we say that people are double-jointed, which doesn’t mean they have two joints instead of one. Double-jointed people are more flexible than the average person because the ligaments between their joints are looser. These loose ligaments allow them to bend in unusual ways.
pages.brief: People bend and twist into different positions, showing how joints are places where bones meet. More than 100 joints let a hard, unbending skeleton move; a flexible person bends unusually because the ligaments between joints are looser, often called double-jointed.

pages.text: An X-ray of the hip joint, which connects the pelvis and femur Not all joints are the same. The joint where the humerus connects to the shoulder bone is a ball-and-socket joint. The connection between the femur and the pelvis is another joint of this type. The top end of the humerus has a ball shape. This ball fits snugly into a round socket in the shoulder. The same is true for the femur, which fits into the pelvis. The elbow joint and the knee joint are hinge joints. Hinge joints can bend in only one direction. The joints between the vertebrae of your spine are swivel joints, which tilt and turn. Sutures connect the skull bones but do not allow much movement. socket ball The hip joint is a ball-and-socket joint.
pages.brief: An X-ray shows the hip joint where the pelvis and femur meet as a ball-and-socket joint. The shoulder has the same ball-and-socket shape, while elbow and knee joints are hinges that bend one way, spine joints tilt and turn, and skull sutures allow little movement.

pages.text: Inside Your Bones It might seem as if bones are hard and dead, like rocks, but that is not the case. Bones are alive with millions of bone cells that need oxygen and food to survive, just like other types of cells. On the outside, a bone is hard and solid. This outer layer is the compact bone. Below the compact bone is the spongy bone, which has holes to keep the bones light so our muscles can lift them. Inside the spongy bone is bone marrow. Bone marrow is the place where the body makes blood cells. The bone marrow in most adults produces more than 50 billion red blood cells every day! bone marrow compact bone spongy bone.
pages.brief: A bone is shown cut open to reveal its living inside: a hard compact outer layer, lighter spongy bone with holes, and bone marrow in the center. Bone cells need oxygen and food, and marrow makes blood cells - more than 50 billion red blood cells a day in most adults.

pages.text: Keeping Bones Healthy Even though bones are very strong, they can break if they are hit hard enough. Healing a broken bone requires a little help from a doctor and a great deal of help from bone cells. For a bone to heal correctly, the bone must be put back the way it was before the break. Doctors may need to move around the broken bones to put them back together. Then they place a cast around the body part where the bone was broken. The cast keeps the body part from moving so the bone has time to heal. As soon as a bone breaks, bone cells begin repairing it. Holding the broken bone in place with a cast allows the bone cells to do their job. A cast helps hold a broken bone in place so it can heal.
pages.brief: A doctor places a cast around a broken body part to hold the bone still while it heals. Bone cells begin repairing the break as soon as it happens, and the cast keeps the broken bone in place so the cells can do their job.

pages.text: Bones need to stay healthy to remain strong. Exercising regularly is the best way to keep bones in good working order. Eating a well-balanced diet helps the bone marrow to produce healthy blood cells. Legumes (such as pinto beans or peas), other vegetables, and fruits are good for bones. Foods rich in calcium, such as dairy products and fortified soy milk, rice milk, and orange juice, can also help bones to grow. Bones give a body its shape, and they also give it much more. They give the body the ability to move, sit, stand, and write. Human bodies wouldn’t be the same without bones! Bones help people do all kinds of fun activities.
pages.brief: People exercise and eat a well-balanced diet with legumes, vegetables, fruits, and calcium-rich foods such as dairy products and fortified soy milk, rice milk, and orange juice. Strong healthy bones give the body shape and let people move, sit, stand, write and enjoy fun activities.

pages.brief: A full human skeleton shows the cranium, clavicle, humerus, rib cage, spinal column, radius, ulna, wrist bones, hand bones, pelvis, femur, fibula, patella, tibia, ankle bones and foot bones, with swivel joints, tendons and vertebrates represented.

books.title: Meteors and Meteorites
books.art_why: Many pages show space objects, past impacts, and Earth's formation that cannot be directly photographed.

pages.text: MEXICO A meteor passes over Reno, Nevada, on the morning of April 22, 2012. The Sky Is Falling The morning of April 22, 2012, began quietly. Suddenly, a ball of fire streaked through the sky over Nevada and California. Hundreds of people on the ground reported seeing the object passing high overhead. Many also heard a loud boom and said that their windows shook. The fast- moving ball of fire shone brightly as it raced through the sunny morning sky. Moments later, the object exploded in the air northeast of Sacramento, California, scattering pieces of itself over a wide area.
pages.brief: A bright ball of fire streaks across a sunny morning sky above Reno, Nevada, and California on April 22, 2012. Below, hundreds of people look up and react as the object passes overhead. The fireball shines intensely, then explodes in the air northeast of Sacramento, California, scattering rocky pieces over a wide area.

pages.text: The flying object that lit up the sky that morning was a hunk of rock from space—a meteor. The meteor broke into pieces over an area of California where the famous gold rush of 1849 began. The minivan-sized meteor’s explosion set off a second gold rush of sorts as thousands of treasure seekers flocked to the area to look for meteorites, or pieces of the meteor, worth more than their weight in gold. Many scientists also rushed to the scene, hoping to recover meteorites that might help them learn more about the origins of our solar system. Their efforts soon paid off as scientists and amateurs alike quickly found pieces of the meteor. Tests revealed that the rocks came from a rare kind of meteor that might be 4.5 billion years old—as old as our solar system. Robert Ward shows two pieces of the California meteor that he found.
pages.brief: A minivan-sized meteor breaks apart over California gold-rush country. Treasure seekers and scientists spread across the area, searching the ground for meteorite pieces. Robert Ward shows two dark rocky pieces he found. The scene suggests a second gold rush as people hunt for space rocks worth more than their weight in gold.

pages.text: Comets, Asteroids, and Meteoroids Where did the California meteor come from? Outer space is full of objects left over from the time when the planets in our solar system formed. Comets, asteroids, and meteoroids are three different kinds of these “leftovers.” Comets are dirty snowballs. They are huge lumps of dirt and rock mixed in with frozen water and gases. Most comets travel through the Kuiper (KY-per) Belt, an area of our solar system located beyond the planets. Asteroids are rocks that range from about the size of a school bus to as large as a small moon. Asteroids mainly orbit the Sun in the asteroid belt, which is between Mars and Jupiter. Most of the space rocks that make their way to Earth come from the Asteroid Belt or the Kuiper Belt. Many comets have large orbits that carry them far beyond the planets. (Drawing not to scale.)
pages.brief: In outer space, a comet appears as a dirty snowball of dirt, rock, frozen water, and gases. Asteroids of many sizes orbit the Sun in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. A meteoroid is shown as a smaller space rock. The drawing compares these three leftovers from the solar system's formation, with distant planets and the Sun.

pages.text: An artist’s drawing shows an asteroid being broken apart by the gravity of a nearby star. Meteoroids are rocks much smaller than comets and asteroids. Some are no bigger than a speck of sand. Others are as large as boulders. A meteoroid becomes a meteor when it hits Earth’s atmosphere. We see meteors as streaks of light racing through the sky—”shooting stars.” When a meteor hits Earth’s surface, scientists call it a meteorite. Meteorites are unlike any rocks on Earth. As our solar system originally took shape, bits of asteroids and planets broke apart. The rocks flew through outer space as meteoroids. Some are still crashing into Earth as meteorites. By studying these space rocks, scientists can figure out how our solar system formed. They can also learn how meteorites have changed our planet.
pages.brief: An artist's drawing shows an asteroid being broken apart by the gravity of a nearby star. Nearby, meteoroids of different sizes float in space, from specks of sand to boulders. One meteoroid hits Earth's atmosphere and becomes a bright streak, a shooting star; another reaches Earth's surface as a meteorite.

pages.text: A Martian Has Landed In 1984, meteorite hunters found a greenish rock in Antarctica. Scientists were shocked when they studied the stone. This was no ordinary meteorite. Tests showed that the rock, about the size of a potato, came from Mars. How did a Martian rock land on Earth some 140 million miles (225 million km) away? Scientists believe an asteroid or comet slammed into Mars 15 million years ago. The crash tossed the rock toward Earth, where it arrived only 13 thousand years ago. Scientists collect a meteorite from the ice in Antarctica.
pages.brief: In Antarctica, scientists collect a greenish meteorite from the ice. The rock is about the size of a potato. A drawing suggests its journey: an asteroid or comet slammed into Mars 15 million years ago, tossing the rock toward Earth, where it arrived 13 thousand years ago after traveling 140 million miles.

pages.text: Scientists estimate that there are 300,000 large impact craters on the side of the Moon that faces Earth. Many more are on the Moon’s far side. Mighty Meteors When people say they’ve seen a shooting star, what they really saw was a blazing meteor streaking through Earth’s atmosphere. The ancient Greeks believed the flashes of light were weapons of the gods. What they didn’t know is that most meteoroids are pieces that have broken away from asteroids. Meteors are chunks of comets and planets. Meteorites can do a lot of damage. Just gaze up at the Moon to see the evidence. The many circular craters on the Moon’s surface are the result of millions of strikes by meteors and comets.
pages.brief: A blazing meteor streaks through Earth's atmosphere above a landscape, appearing as a shooting star. In the sky, the Moon shows many circular craters from millions of strikes by meteors and comets. The scene contrasts Earth's protected surface with the Moon's cratered face, which has no atmosphere to shield it.

pages.text: Since there is no atmosphere on the Moon, there’s nothing to protect its surface from these flying space rocks. Luckily, Earth has an atmosphere that shields our planet. When a meteor collides with Earth’s atmosphere, the fast-moving rock pushes air out of its way. As air particles move past the surface of a meteor at high speed, they cause the meteor to heat up and break into pieces. As those pieces burn up, the meteor glows in brilliant, fiery streaks of light. Then it vanishes as quickly as it appeared. 1. A fast-moving meteor enters the atmosphere. 2. It rubs against the air, causing it to heat up and glow. 3. The meteor leaves behind a trail of melting rock and hot gases. 4. Most meteors break apart and burn up in the air before reaching the ground.
pages.brief: A fast-moving meteor enters Earth's atmosphere. It rubs against the air, heats up, and glows brightly. It leaves behind a trail of melting rock and hot gases. Most meteors break apart and burn up in the air before reaching the ground, with the fiery streak vanishing as quickly as it appeared.

pages.text: Fireballs and Micrometeorites On February 2, 2012, residents of Amarillo, Texas, heard a loud boom at around 8:00 p.m. When people looked up, they saw a blazing meteor light up the sky. What people saw was a special type of meteor that scientists call a fireball. Because some meteoroids are huge, they grow extremely bright when striking the atmosphere. In fact, some get as bright as the Moon for a short time. This fireball, seen over California’s Mojave Desert in 2009, was caused by a meteor that was once part of a comet.
pages.brief: Over California's Mojave Desert in 2009, a fireball blazes across the sky. It is a special meteor that grew extremely bright after striking the atmosphere, once part of a comet. In Amarillo, Texas, on February 2, 2012, residents heard a loud boom at around 8:00 p.m. and looked up to see a blazing meteor.

pages.text: A U.S. Navy fighter jet breaks the sound barrier, causing water droplets to form clouds in the shape of shock waves. What was the blast that everyone heard? The fireball was moving faster than the speed of sound, which is roughly 760 miles (1,223 km) per hour. As the object raced through the atmosphere, it shattered the sound barrier. Kaboom! The noise that shook Amarillo was a sonic boom. Sonic booms can be low, rumbling sounds or ear- splitting explosions. The noise can shake the ground and even break windows. Fireballs are rare. Micrometeorites are not. Most of these tiny meteors are smaller than a freckle. Tons of micrometeorites pass through the air and fall to Earth every year.
pages.brief: A U.S. Navy fighter jet breaks the sound barrier, and water droplets form clouds shaped like shock waves around it. The scene explains the sonic boom heard in Amarillo: a fireball racing faster than sound shook the ground and broke windows. Tiny micrometeorites, smaller than freckles, fall through the air to Earth in huge numbers.

pages.text: Some meteor showers produce more than one meteor per minute. Meteor Showers What type of shower won’t get you wet? A meteor shower, of course! Meteor showers are brief periods of heavy meteor activity. They are fun to watch, and you don’t need an umbrella. Most meteor showers happen at the same time every year. They are often named after the constellation in which they seem to appear. For example, every November the Leonid meteor shower appears in the same area of the sky as the constellation Leo. Hundreds, sometimes thousands, of meteors can streak across the sky every hour.
pages.brief: A meteor shower fills the night sky with many bright streaks. Some showers produce more than one meteor per minute. The meteors appear near a constellation, such as the Leonid shower appearing every November in the same sky area as Leo. Hundreds, sometimes thousands, of meteors can streak across the sky every hour.

pages.text: Scientists know when meteor showers will happen because they begin each time Earth passes behind a comet. As the comet closes in on the Sun, it leaves a “tail” of dust and melting ice behind it in space. When Earth passes through the comet’s tail, the dust burns up in the atmosphere, creating a natural fireworks show. Gas tail Energy from the Sun Dust tail A comet leaves behind a tail of dust and gas as it moves through space.
pages.brief: In space, a comet leaves a tail of dust and gas behind as it moves toward the Sun. Energy from the Sun affects the comet, creating a dust tail and a gas tail. Earth passes through the comet's tail, and the dust burns up in the atmosphere, creating a natural fireworks show of meteors.

pages.text: Space Gold Scientists say an ancient meteor shower is the reason gold can be found in the rocks near Earth’s surface. Why do they say that? When Earth began forming around 4.5 billion years ago, it was a big ball of molten rock. As Earth cooled, iron sank to the center of the planet, forming Earth’s core. Some other metals, including gold, sank with the iron. Crust Mantle Solid inner core Liquid outer core Scientists estimate that 99 percent of Earth’s gold sank to its core when our planet was still forming.
pages.brief: A cutaway view of Earth shows its crust, mantle, solid inner core, and liquid outer core. Long ago, when Earth was a ball of molten rock, iron and other metals, including gold, sank to the center. Scientists estimate that 99 percent of Earth's gold sank to its core while the planet was still forming.

pages.text: Did these gold nuggets journey to Earth from space? If all the gold sank, scientists wondered, where do we find the gold to make watches, bracelets, and other items? About 650 million years after Earth formed, a firestorm of meteorites rained down. That meteor shower forever changed the makeup of Earth’s crust. Scientists say that so many meteorites slammed into our planet that if you put them all together, they would weigh about one-fourth as much as Earth’s moon. Most of the gold we use for jewelry and coins came from those meteorites.
pages.brief: Gold nuggets rest in rock, with a question of whether they journeyed to Earth from space. About 650 million years after Earth formed, a firestorm of meteorites rained down and changed the makeup of Earth's crust. Most of the gold used for jewelry and coins came from those meteorites, which together would weigh about one-fourth as much as the Moon.

pages.text: Types of Meteorites Meteorites can give us clues as to how our solar system formed. Yet, not all meteorites are the same. Meteorites come in three main types. Nearly all meteorites are stone. Some stony meteorites come from the Moon or Mars. A few contain small, glassy beads, which formed under high heat at the time the solar system began to form. Iron meteorites come from the core of a long- vanished asteroid or planet. These meteorites are dark and look as if they are rusting. Iron meteorites are very heavy and sometimes have surfaces that look the way a lump of clay looks after being pressed all over with fingertips. Early humans made tools and weapons out of the iron meteorites they found. How Common Is Each Type of Meteorite? Stony-iron meteorites 1% Iron meteorites 7% Stony meteorites 92%.
pages.brief: Meteorites are shown in three main types: stony, iron, and stony-iron. Nearly all meteorites are stone, and some stony meteorites come from the Moon or Mars or contain glassy beads. Iron meteorites are dark, heavy, and look rusting, from the core of a vanished asteroid or planet. Stony-iron meteorites are rare mixes of stone and iron.

pages.text: Arizona’s Barringer Crater was created by an iron meteorite approximately 50,000 years ago. Stony-iron are the last type of meteorites. If you find one, you’re lucky. Stony-iron meteorites are rare. As their name suggests, these space rocks are a mix of stone and iron. Meteorite impacts can be devastating. On land, a meteorite strike can create a gigantic explosion and powerful shock waves. Fortunately, the most destructive meteorite impacts happened long ago. Not only does Earth’s atmosphere protect the planet, but the pull of the Moon’s gravity steers some meteoroids away from us.
pages.brief: Arizona's Barringer Crater appears as a huge bowl in the land, created by an iron meteorite about 50,000 years ago. A stony-iron meteorite is shown as a rare mix of stone and iron. On land, a meteorite strike can create a gigantic explosion and powerful shock waves, but Earth's atmosphere and the Moon's gravity help protect the planet.

pages.text: Dying Dinos Scientists say, however, that some 65 million years ago, one very large meteorite got through. At the time, Earth was home to many kinds of dinosaurs. After the large meteorite struck Earth, the dinosaurs vanished. Earth turned into a wasteland. Although scientists aren’t completely sure, they believe a massive meteorite or asteroid strike blasted the dinosaurs into extinction. Scientists say the impact threw huge amounts of dust, gas, and rock into the air. The blast changed Earth’s climate, killing almost everything.
pages.brief: Long ago, many kinds of dinosaurs lived on Earth. A very large meteorite or asteroid strikes, throwing huge amounts of dust, gas, and rock into the air. The blast changes Earth's climate and turns the land into a wasteland, and the dinosaurs vanish. Scientists believe this impact caused their extinction.

pages.text: United States GULF OF MEXICO Giant meteorite crater Mexico Yucatán Why do scientists say a meteorite was the cause? One possible answer comes from scientists who study layers of rock on Earth’s surface. They noticed that at the same time the dinosaurs disappeared, the amount of iridium (ih-RIH-dee- um) on the planet went up dramatically. Iridium is a metal that is rare on Earth but is common elsewhere in our solar system. The sudden increase of iridium in Earth’s rock layers made scientists suspect that a large meteorite slammed into Earth, bringing a huge amount of iridium with it.
pages.brief: A map-like drawing shows the Gulf of Mexico, Mexico, the Yucatán, and the United States, with a giant meteorite crater near the Yucatán. Layers of rock on Earth's surface show a dramatic rise in iridium at the same time the dinosaurs disappeared. Iridium is rare on Earth but common elsewhere in the solar system, suggesting a large meteorite struck.

pages.text: Asteroid Mining While some people see giant rocks in space as a threat, others see them as an opportunity. A company called Planetary Resources wants to send spacecraft to mine asteroids in space. According to the company, more than 1,500 asteroids orbit near Earth and could be easily reached using today’s technology. Asteroids contain many valuable resources including precious metals and rare minerals. Asteroids may also contain a resource that’s particularly valuable in space—water. Target Earth? The chances of another giant meteorite coming our way are slim. In 1908, a meteorite blew apart over the Tunguska River in Siberia. The blast leveled 400 square miles (1,000 sq km) of forest. Had the meteorite struck a city, the destruction would have been massive. However, we shouldn’t worry too much. Scientists say chances are that a large meteorite will hit a major city only about once every 10,000 years.
pages.brief: A spacecraft travels toward asteroids in space, illustrating a company's plan to mine asteroids for precious metals, rare minerals, and water. More than 1,500 asteroids orbit near Earth. In 1908, a meteorite blew apart over the Tunguska River in Siberia, leveling 400 square miles of forest. A large meteorite hitting a major city is rare, about once every 10,000 years.

pages.text: Yet, meteorites continue to fall and always will. If you look up in the sky tonight, you might see a meteor streak across the horizon as it ends its journey through space and time in a blazing show of light.
pages.brief: A meteor streaks across the horizon in the night sky, ending its journey through space and time in a blazing show of light. Stars fill the dark sky above a quiet landscape. Meteorites continue to fall and always will, so tonight someone might see a bright streak overhead.

books.title: The Secret Service
books.art_why: The book covers 1800s assassinations and early history where real photographs of the events are impossible.

pages.text: The Obamas walk to the White House on Inauguration Day 2009. Introduction All eyes were on Washington D.C.’s newest couple—the Obamas. It was January 21, 2009. Barack Obama had just been sworn in as the first Black president of the United States. The new president smiled as he walked down Pennsylvania Avenue to the White House. He held hands with the First Lady, Michelle Obama. The couple waved to the cheering crowd. Nearby, groups of people dressed in dark suits, some wearing sunglasses, moved along with the couple. Unlike most people in the crowd, these individuals were not looking at the new president and First Lady. Instead, their eyes were searching the crowd of people lining the street, looking for any hint of danger. They were agents of the U.S. Secret Service.
pages.brief: Barack and Michelle Obama walk hand in hand down Pennsylvania Avenue toward the White House on Inauguration Day 2009, smiling and waving to a cheering crowd. Around them, dark-suited Secret Service agents with sunglasses scan the people lining the street for danger.

pages.text: Even though it was freezing cold outside, the agents had their suit jackets open and their hands close to their hidden weapons. They had sworn an oath to protect the president and had been planning for Inauguration Day for months. The agents left nothing to chance. They had blocked many of Washington’s streets and added security checkpoints. Soldiers kept careful watch from the tops of buildings. Fighter jets circled overhead. Boats patrolled the Potomac River. Secret Service agents closed off the streets to provide security during the Obama inauguration.
pages.brief: In freezing weather, Secret Service agents keep their suit jackets open and their hands near hidden weapons. Washington streets are blocked with security checkpoints. Soldiers watch from building rooftops, fighter jets circle overhead, and boats patrol the Potomac River near the inauguration route.

pages.text: The door of “The Beast” reveals its thick armor. Agents even built the president a new car, which they nicknamed “The Beast.” It looked like a black limousine, but it was really a tank. Its eight inches of armor could protect the Obamas from just about anything. All day, agents stuck close to the first couple as the Obamas made their way from the inaugural parade to dances and balls. Nothing bad happened. That’s the way it was supposed to be. The planning and hard work of the Secret Service had paid off. It was all in a day’s work.
