Some animals build to protect themselves or to catch prey, while others build to attract a mate. A bowerbird spruces up his bower with blue feathers and plastic. To woo females, the male birds first build the bower, then decorate it!
pages.brief: A male bowerbird spruces up his bower with blue feathers and plastic, then decorates it to woo females. The bower is his built structure, and the scene shows him arranging the bright blue items at the bower. He is the animal builder, working to attract a mate.

pages.text: Welcome to Tunnel Town The largest known prairie dog town, in Texas, covered 25,000 square miles (65,000 sq km). It was home to as many as 400 million prairie dogs! Prairie Dog Towns Prairie dog burrows are like real towns. Their maze of underground tunnels has different rooms for sleeping, eating, and even going to the bathroom! Family groups stay together in separate areas or “neighborhoods” that include many entrances. Prairie dogs spend a lot of time building and fixing their homes. Prairie dogs are only found in North America.
pages.brief: Prairie dogs live in a large town of burrows. Their maze of underground tunnels has separate rooms for sleeping, eating, and going to the bathroom. Family groups stay together in neighborhoods with many entrances, and the prairie dogs spend time building and fixing their homes.

pages.text: Sociable weavers live in southern Africa. Their nests help protect them from hot and cold outside temperatures. Sociable Weaver Bird Nests The more the merrier for these friendly birds. They build the biggest nests of any birds—their nests can hold up to four hundred birds. They use large sticks and dry grass for the nest’s roof and sides. Inside, separate living areas are lined with softer grasses and fibers.
pages.brief: Sociable weavers in southern Africa build the biggest nests of any bird. Large sticks and dry grass form the roof and sides of a nest that can hold up to four hundred birds. Inside, separate living areas are lined with softer grasses and fibers, helping protect the birds from hot and cold temperatures.

pages.text: Termite Mounds Tiny termites can build structures that are taller than three people standing on top of each other! They build their mounds from mud, chewed wood, and saliva. The walls have tiny holes for fresh air. The termite mounds even have a chimney and a cellar. The termites build many storage areas for wood, their main food source. One Queen, 165 Million Eggs! The king and queen termite live in a special chamber. The queen can produce thousands of eggs per day and can live up to age forty-five. Worker termites carry her young to a nursery room where they are fed until they are adults.
pages.brief: Tiny termites build a tall mound from mud, chewed wood, and saliva. The walls have tiny holes for fresh air, and the mound includes a chimney and a cellar. Inside, storage areas hold wood, while worker termites carry the queen's young to a nursery room to be fed.

pages.text: Pufferfish Circles These male fish create detailed sand art to attract females. They flap their fins on the seafloor to form a large round pattern. Then, they decorate the outer part of the circle with shells. If a female likes the circle, she lays her eggs in the middle.
pages.brief: A male pufferfish flaps his fins on the seafloor to form a large round sand circle. He decorates the outer part of the circle with shells. If a female likes the circle, she lays her eggs in the middle.

pages.text: A trapdoor spider darts from its mossy hiding place. Spider Trapdoors These sly spiders dig an underground tunnel, then make a trapdoor in the tunnel to catch prey. They cover the trapdoor with their silk, and cover that with dirt. When they hear prey passing above them, they open the door and the prey falls through. The door also protects the spiders from animals that hunt them.
pages.brief: A trapdoor spider darts from its mossy hiding place. It has dug an underground tunnel with a trapdoor covered in silk and dirt. When the spider hears prey passing above, it opens the door so the prey falls through; the door also protects the spider from animals that hunt it.

pages.text: Underground Ant City Millions of ants work together to build underground ant cities. These giant cities have dirt “highways” and main paths that connect rooms. Side roads lead to gardens and trash pits, and tunnels allow air to flow. These tiny ants lift many times their own weight to build their huge cities. After humans, leafcutter ants (inset) form the largest communities of any animal on Earth.
pages.brief: Millions of ants work together to build an underground ant city. Dirt highways and main paths connect rooms, while side roads lead to gardens and trash pits. Tunnels allow air to flow. The tiny ants lift many times their own weight to build their huge city.

pages.text: Little Ants, Big City Researchers found a huge, empty underground city in Brazil, once the home of leafcutter ants. In order to build their home, each insect would have carried loads of earth more than half a mile (0.8 km)—over and over. In total, the ants moved around 45 tons (40 mt) of soil to create their network of tunnels. Ants at Work.
pages.brief: A huge, empty underground city in Brazil, once the home of leafcutter ants, is shown with its network of tunnels. Each insect would have carried loads of earth more than half a mile, over and over, and the ants moved around forty-five tons of soil in total.

pages.text: Paper Wasp Nests Paper wasps gather bits of wood and plants. They chew them into a pulp, then spit out the pulp to make a soft nest. The nest is made up of cells that look like an egg carton. Wasp eggs develop in the cells. As the wasps grow in number, the nest gets bigger.
pages.brief: Paper wasps gather bits of wood and plants and chew them into a pulp, then spit out the pulp to make a soft nest. The nest is made up of cells that look like an egg carton. Wasp eggs develop in the cells, and the nest gets bigger as the wasps grow in number.

pages.text: Crayfish Chimneys In order to reach water, some crayfish burrow into moist soil, pushing up wet dirt. The raised soil looks like a small chimney. Since the center of the chimney is empty, other animals, such as snakes, sometimes hide there. Crayfish (also known as crawfish) breathe with gills. Gills must remain wet, which is why crayfish burrow down in search of water.
pages.brief: A crayfish burrows into moist soil, pushing up wet dirt that looks like a small chimney. The center of the chimney is empty, so animals such as snakes sometimes hide there. Crayfish breathe with gills that must remain wet, which is why they burrow down in search of water.

pages.text: The Best of Both Worlds underwater entrances Beavers enter their dens by swimming into them, but their living space is built above the water level. This keeps the beaver family high and dry! Beaver Dams and Dens Beavers are master builders, so if you are “busy as a beaver,” you are very busy. Beavers gather sticks and mud to build their dams. The dams create ponds. Beavers build their homes, called dens, on the ponds to protect themselves from predators. The ponds also make it easier for beavers to store food during the winter.
pages.brief: Beavers gather sticks and mud to build dams that create ponds. They build their homes, called dens, on the ponds, with underwater entrances, but the living space is above the water level. This keeps the beaver family high and dry and protects them from predators.

pages.text: Caddisfly Larvae Cocoons These little larvae use their silk to make cocoons. The larvae add sand, small sticks, even shells to their cocoons to make beautiful artlike cases. Watch Them Build Animals build great things and do not need tools to do it. They use their bodies, natural skills, and the Earth’s resources to build their structures. Animals are amazing! A black-tailed prairie dog looks out of its burrow.
pages.brief: Caddisfly larvae use their silk to make cocoons. They add sand, small sticks, and even shells to their cocoons to make beautiful artlike cases. A black-tailed prairie dog looks out of its burrow. The animals use their bodies, natural skills, and the Earth's resources to build their structures without tools.

books.title: Strange Plants
books.art_why: Real plants and natural habitats can be photographed.

pages.text: When we think about plants, we often think of trees, flowers, bushes, and grass. We usually think about organisms that have stems, leaves, roots, and sometimes flowers. Most plants, such as the ones in this photograph, have roots that grow into the ground.
pages.brief: A view of ordinary plants such as trees, flowers, bushes, and grass, which have stems, leaves, roots, and sometimes flowers. These plants grow with roots reaching down into the ground, keeping them fixed in the soil.

pages.text: While the majority of plants have these four basic components, some plants are different. This book explores some of these strange plants.
pages.brief: An introduction to strange plants: a few unusual plants are shown alongside ordinary plants that have basic parts—stems, leaves, roots, and sometimes flowers—to show that some plants are different from the majority and are explored here.

pages.text: Plants commonly called air plants live in trees high above the ground near ponds, streams, rivers, and swamps in North and South America. Their roots aren’t buried in dirt, as is the case with most plants; instead, the plants grow on tree branches. They take all their nutrients and moisture from the air, through their leaves. They use their roots to anchor themselves to branches— not to obtain nutrients.
pages.brief: Air plants growing on tree branches high above the ground near ponds, streams, rivers, or swamps in North or South America. Their roots are attached to branches, not buried in dirt, and their leaves take moisture and nutrients from the air.

pages.text: Unbelievable though it may seem, there are several large groups of carnivorous, or meat- eating, plants. They eat insects, spiders, and even some fish, amphibians, reptiles, and small mammals. Like all plants, they use sunlight and water to make their own food in a process called photosynthesis. The animals they “eat” help them survive because these plants live in places where the soil doesn’t supply enough nutrients.
pages.brief: Carnivorous plants in nutrient-poor soil, with leaves ready to catch insects, spiders, and even small fish, amphibians, reptiles, or small mammals. Sunlight and water surround them as they make their own food, while the animals they capture help them survive.

pages.text: One well-known meat-eating plant is the Venus flytrap, which lives in moist environments. Its leaves look like traps. The traps have small trigger hairs on the inside. When a critter walks inside a leaf and brushes against the trigger hairs, the leaf snaps shut. The critter is then trapped.
pages.brief: A Venus flytrap in a moist environment, its leaves shaped like open traps with small trigger hairs inside. A small critter walks inside one leaf and brushes the trigger hairs, and the leaf snaps shut around it, trapping the critter.

pages.text: The sundew, another meat-eating plant that lives in moist environments, catches its food in a different way. It has many sticky hairs on its surface that smell sweet. Insects attracted to the smell land and get stuck. Then the plant digests the insects. The giant sundew plant of Australia, which can grow to 1 meter (3.28 ft.) tall, even eats small frogs!
pages.brief: A sundew in a moist environment, covered with many sticky hairs that smell sweet. An insect lands on the sticky surface and gets stuck as the plant digests it. A giant sundew from Australia, able to grow one meter tall, catches even small frogs.

pages.text: Some plants steal food from other plants. The dodder plant lives on many continents but is most common in North and South America. It sends slender rootlike stems into another plant. These stems are pale green, yellow, or bright orange and are easy to see against the host plant. The dodder sucks food and water from the plant. It is a parasite—a living thing that lives off another living thing. When a dodder plant attaches to a host plant, its connection to the soil dies.
pages.brief: A dodder plant with slender rootlike stems in pale green, yellow, or bright orange, attached to a host plant. The dodder sends its stems into the host and draws food and water from it, while its own connection to the soil dies.

pages.text: Many flowers have bad smells that attract insects. The stapelia flower, also called the “carrion flower,” emits an odor of rotting meat. On hot days, the odor is noticeable from about 1.6 kilometers (1 mi.) away. The flower has a pattern that looks like dead animals. Flies are attracted to the pattern and the smell, so they fly into the flower. Special powder called “pollen” gets on their bodies. They carry the powder to other flowers, which use it to reproduce.
pages.brief: A stapelia flower, also called a carrion flower, with a pattern that looks like dead animals and an odor of rotting meat noticeable on hot days. Flies fly into the flower, pick up pollen on their bodies, and carry it to other flowers.

pages.text: Some plants look like rocks. The plants in the photograph above are called “stone plants” or “living stones.” They live in very hot, dry places such as South Africa. They hold water very well because the biggest part of each plant lives underground. They rarely grow more than 2.5 centimeters (1 in.) above the ground and have only two leaves. Once each year, these plants usually grow a white or yellow flower. Their shape helps to hide them so animals do not eat them.
pages.brief: Stone plants, or living stones, in a very hot, dry place in South Africa. Most of each plant lives underground, with only two leaves rarely more than 2.5 centimeters above ground, and a white or yellow flower once each year; their shape helps hide them from animals.

pages.text: Some cactus plants are covered with wool-like hairs. These plants come from Bolivia and Peru, high in the Andes Mountains of South America. The “wool” protects them from daytime heat and nighttime cold. The “wool” also helps the cactus plants hold moisture.
pages.brief: Cactus plants covered with wool-like hairs in Bolivia and Peru, high in the Andes Mountains of South America. The wool protects them from daytime heat and nighttime cold and helps the cactus plants hold moisture.

pages.text: Some trees and shrubs grow out of solid rock. They grow up high where the wind blows strong. The wind can blow seeds into small cracks in the rock. When rain gets into the cracks, the seeds start to grow. Their roots reach down into small cracks for moisture. Once the roots are stable, the plants grow leaves to absorb sunlight and are then able to keep growing. As the roots grow, they split the rock.
pages.brief: Trees and shrubs growing out of solid rock high where the wind blows strong. Seeds blown into small cracks sprout when rain gets in; roots reach down for moisture, leaves absorb sunlight, and the growing roots split the rock.

pages.text: Some plants have animals living inside them. Ant colonies live within ant plants. The ants protect the plant from animals that would eat it. The ants use natural cavities, or spaces, in the plant’s stem as houses. Some spaces are used for raising young ants. Other spaces are used for garbage. The ant plant uses some of this garbage for food and to spread its seeds.
pages.brief: An ant plant with ant colonies living inside natural cavities in its stem. Some spaces hold young ants and others hold garbage; the ants protect the plant from animals that would eat it, and the plant uses some garbage for food and to spread its seeds.

pages.text: There are many more kinds of strange plants. Bamboo makes noise when it grows. Some Australian orchids grow and flower completely underground. Bat plants have fruit that looks like bats hanging upside down from the flowers. Some ghost plants have white flowers that seem to appear out of nowhere. There are many amazing plants in the world. Bamboo shoots.
pages.brief: More strange plants: bamboo shoots making noise as bamboo grows, Australian orchids growing and flowering completely underground, bat plants with fruit that looks like bats hanging upside down from flowers, and ghost plants with white flowers that seem to appear out of nowhere.

books.title: Labor Day
books.art_why: The book covers labor history from the 1800s and early 1900s, when real photos of many events are impossible.

pages.text: Labor Day.
pages.brief: A plain opening page for a book about Labor Day, with an open space that sets the stage for a look at workers, parades, and the holiday’s history. No people or objects are described on the page, so the opening image remains simple and uncluttered.

pages.text: Marchers in a parade in honor of union workers. Back to School In the United States, Labor Day is the first Monday in September. It’s time to enjoy one last blast of summer fun. Government offices and many businesses close. Some people get the day off work. Some throw parties. Labor Day isn’t just a day to take it easy, though. It’s also a day to honor American workers. To understand what Labor Day honors, it’s important to learn about the history of workers in the United States.
pages.brief: Marchers in a parade honoring union workers walk together in celebration. Elsewhere people enjoy one last blast of summer fun, with some off work and some at parties, while government offices and many businesses close for the first Monday in September.

pages.text: Horses did much of the work in the time before machines. Machines and Workers In the late 1700s and early 1800s, many new kinds of machines were invented. People who had money to buy the machines started to make more money. However, machines now did jobs that people used to do. Many people moved to cities and went to work in factories. They no longer had any other way to make money. Many factory owners wanted to pay workers as little as possible. Workers often lost their jobs if they asked for more money. In the 1800s, low pay, long working hours, and unsafe workplaces were common. A farmer plows a field in 1925.
pages.brief: A farmer plows a field in 1925 with horses doing much of the work, showing the time before machines. New machines from the late 1700s and early 1800s are invented and used in factories, as many people move to cities and take factory jobs for low pay.

pages.text: Tough Jobs Many workers in the 1800s got little time off work. The United States had no rules about how many hours people could work. Many factory workers worked 100 hours a week! Workers who did not like this could lose their jobs. Women and children work in a factory in 1911.
pages.brief: Women and children work in a factory in 1911, standing among machines and doing jobs for long hours. The scene shows tough jobs in the 1800s, when workers got little time off and many factory workers worked up to 100 hours a week.

pages.text: Children work in a tobacco factory in 1917. Child Labor By the early 1800s, about two million children were working in factories in the United States. Many were from families with too little money to support them. Children often held jobs before age ten. Some were as young as six or seven. They worked six days a week, up to eighteen hours each day. This left little time for rest and no time for school or play. Many children became ill as a result.
pages.brief: Children work in a tobacco factory in 1917, doing factory jobs at workstations. The scene shows child labor: young workers, some as young as six or seven, labored six days a week for up to eighteen hours, with little rest and no time for school or play.

pages.text: Workers Join Together Over time, workers wanted more of a say in how they were treated. Groups of workers came together to form labor unions. They did this to protect their rights as workers. Labor unions help get companies to agree to better hours, pay, and safer workplaces. Unions sometimes call for workers to stop working, or strike, to get a better deal at their jobs. In 1869, President Ulysses S. Grant made a new rule that government workers only had to work eight hours each day. Soon after, people started working to get a law passed that would do the same for all workers. Many unions have their own seal that they put on things they work on or make. Union seals are a mark of pride. They also let shoppers know what goods were made by union workers.
pages.brief: Workers join together in groups to form labor unions, standing as a united group to protect their rights and ask for better hours, pay, and safer workplaces. A union seal is shown as a mark of pride that lets shoppers know which goods were made by union workers.

pages.text: Women were mostly left out of the early labor movement. But women were still fighting for voting rights and fair working conditions. One step forward for women’s rights was when clothing workers in New York City formed a big union. They showed that women were important to the labor movement. Labor Unions Today Union membership across the United States has dropped since the 1980s. However, starting in 2020, strikes and unionization efforts have been rising. Unions for government workers are steadily growing. Teachers, postal workers, firefighters, and police officers all have strong unions. As of 2024, about 9.9% of workers in the United States are part of a union.
pages.brief: Women clothing workers in New York City form a big union, standing together to show that women are important to the labor movement. Nearby, today’s union members include teachers, postal workers, firefighters, and police officers, as strikes and unionization efforts rise after 2020.

pages.text: Help from Congress In 1938, Congress passed an important set of laws to help workers. The laws said a workweek could not be more than forty-four hours. (It was changed to forty hours two years later.) The laws also set the lowest pay allowed. The laws helped make sure workers earned at least enough money to meet their basic needs. Minimum Wage When the Fair Labor Standards Act passed in 1938, the minimum wage was $0.25 per hour. (Today, that would be $5.03.) In 2025, the U.S. minimum wage was $7.25 per hour. States are free to set it higher, and 30 states and Washington D.C. have.
pages.brief: Members of Congress pass laws in 1938 to help workers, setting a workweek of no more than forty-four hours and a minimum wage of $0.25 per hour. The page shows the minimum wage changing over time, reaching $7.25 per hour in 2025, with some states setting it higher.

pages.text: Math Minute A worker’s rate of pay is $15.00 per hour. How much does that worker earn in a forty-hour workweek? How much do they earn in a week with ten hours of overtime? The laws also said hourly workers had to be paid extra when they worked more than forty hours each week. Workers earn one-and-a-half times their usual hourly rate for each extra hour they work. These laws were meant to keep companies from forcing people to work too many hours. The laws also made safety rules and said that young children could not work at many types of jobs. Children now had to be sixteen years old to work during school hours. They could be fourteen for some after-school jobs. During the 1894 Pullman Strike, railroad workers struck for over two months because of wage cuts that hurt their families.
pages.brief: A worker calculates pay at $15.00 per hour for a forty-hour week and for ten hours of overtime. Railroad workers during the 1894 Pullman Strike stand together for over two months after wage cuts hurt their families, while laws set extra pay for overtime and safety rules for young workers.

pages.text: Key People in the Labor Movement Mother Jones (Mary Harris Jones, 1837–1930) helped coal miners in the early 1900s. Union members called her “Mother” because of her hard work on their behalf. She traveled across the United States to help striking miners and to end child labor. A. Philip Randolph (1889-1979) was an advocate for Black working class interests in the United States. He led a ten-year drive to organize the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters. These workers took care of passengers during train trips. Randolph also called for a march on Washington to protest employment discrimination in the armed forces. His commitment to non-violent protest and mass actions efforts helped inspire the civil rights movement of the 1950s and 60s. Eugene Debs (1855–1926) helped found unions for railroad workers and industrial workers. He ran for president five times between 1900 and 1920. Debs traveled the country helping workers bargain with their employers. Dolores Huerta (born 1930) is the co-founder of the United Farm Workers Association. She focused her work on low-income families, women, and children. In 1965, Huerta helped organize a strike of 5,000 grape farmers. She helped negotiate a contract that provided safer conditions. She traveled across the United States supporting campaigns and promoting equal rights legislation and policies.
pages.brief: Drawings show four key people in the labor movement: Mother Jones, who helped coal miners and fought child labor; A. Philip Randolph, who organized sleeping car porters; Eugene Debs, who helped found railroad and industrial unions; and Dolores Huerta, co-founder of the United Farm Workers Association.

pages.text: Workers march on Labor Day in 1882 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. A New Holiday Labor Day was first celebrated in New York City in 1882. In 1887, Oregon became the first state to pass a law making Labor Day a holiday. Thirty more states did the same before the U.S. government made Labor Day a holiday for the whole nation in 1894.
pages.brief: Workers march on Labor Day in 1882 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, walking together in a parade. The scene marks a new holiday first celebrated in New York City in 1882, then made a state holiday by Oregon in 1887, and finally a national holiday in 1894.

pages.text: Canada also celebrates Labor Day on the first Monday in September. More than sixty other countries instead celebrate a holiday to honor workers on May 1. On these holidays, people around the world learn about their labor rights. Canadian ironworkers march during a Labor Day parade.
pages.brief: Canadian ironworkers march during a Labor Day parade, walking together in a group. Canada celebrates Labor Day on the first Monday in September, while more than sixty other countries honor workers on May 1 and use the holidays to learn about labor rights.

pages.text: The American Welding Society was founded in 1919. Welders have to use safety equipment to protect themselves while they work. A Better Future Today, labor movements continue to help workers. The COVID-19 pandemic, which arrived in the United States in early 2020, brought attention to certain groups of workers. To support these workers, many have called to raise the lowest possible pay. In 2022, the United States raised the lowest pay for government workers to $15 an hour. For all other workers, it stayed at $7.25 an hour. On Labor Day, take a moment to honor the workers who build better lives for themselves and their communities.
pages.brief: Welders use safety equipment to protect themselves while they work, and the American Welding Society is shown as founded in 1919. In a better future, people honor workers on Labor Day and call for higher pay after the COVID-19 pandemic brought attention to certain groups of workers.

books.title: United Arab Emirates
books.art_why: Modern country, landmarks and people exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: United Arab Emirates Where Is It? The United Arab Emirates (UAE) covers about 83,600 square kilometers (32,278 sq. mi.) of the Arabian Peninsula, which is in the Middle East. The Middle East is the area where Europe, Africa, and Asia meet. Saudi Arabia and Oman border the UAE. A small part of the UAE’s coast lies directly on the Indian Ocean. The rest runs along the Persian Gulf, which is called the Arabian Gulf by the people in the region. In all, the UAE has 1,318 kilometers (819 mi.) of coastline.
pages.brief: A wide satellite view of the Arabian Peninsula shows the United Arab Emirates beside Saudi Arabia and Oman, where Europe, Africa, and Asia meet. Its long coastline runs along the Persian Gulf, with a small part touching the Indian Ocean.

pages.text: The UAE is made up of seven Arab states: Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah (SHAR-juh), Ajman (ej-MAHN), Umm al Quwain (OOM AHL ky- WAYN), Ras al Khaimah (RAHS AHL KY-muh), and Al Fujairah (AHL foo-JY-ruh). Each state has its own capital city, which shares the name of the state. The country’s capital city is Abu Dhabi, which lies on an island in the gulf. Abu Dhabi is the UAE’s second-largest city. Its history dates back to 3,000 bce. Abu Dhabi blends its ancient culture with modern buildings. Beautiful white-domed mosques and shining skyscrapers decorate the city. Northeast of Abu Dhabi is the country’s largest city, Dubai—a center for banking, trade, and tourists. It is home to the world’s tallest building, the largest dancing fountain, and one of the largest human-made islands. Do You Know? Dubai is one of the fastest- growing cities in the world. In 1968, there were just 13 cars in the entire city. Today, planners are building double-decker roads for the city’s 1.4 million vehicles. A modern roadway in Dubai.
pages.brief: Abu Dhabi spreads across an island in the gulf, with white-domed mosques beside shining skyscrapers. In Dubai, the world's tallest building, a large dancing fountain, and a human-made island stand near busy modern roads that carry the city's growing traffic.

pages.text: People While millions of people live in the UAE, most are not citizens. People from other countries make up a large part of the UAE’s population. Most of these people came from other Arab countries or from South Asia to work in the country’s successful oil and construction industries. UAE citizens, called Emirati, come from Arab tribes that settled in the area long ago. Though these tribes have often fought, many share certain traditions. For example, they prefer traditional Arab clothing. The lightweight clothing honors their culture and provides comfort in the high heat. For men, traditional clothing is a long, white, cotton, ankle- length robe, a head covering, and a light scarf (either white or red checkered). A UAE family poses for a portrait. Children wear traditional clothing at more formal occasions.
pages.brief: A UAE family poses for a portrait, with adults in traditional Arab clothing and children dressed in traditional outfits for a formal occasion. Men wear long white cotton robes, head coverings, and light scarves, clothing that honors culture and gives comfort in high heat.

pages.text: Worshipers pray in a mosque in Dubai. Women have two kinds of traditional clothing. At home, they may wear a dress with loose pants. Outside, they wear a dark robe and cover their head, and sometimes also their face, with a scarf. For both men and women, head coverings are a sign of respect for their religion. People of the UAE share the religion of Islam. Muslims make up seventy-five percent of the population. Arabic is the official language, but most people also speak local dialects. Because many people move to the UAE from other countries, other languages are common, especially English. Most people live in cities and towns along the UAE coast. Due to the success of the oil industry, the country has grown rich. Builders have put up apartment buildings, schools, hospitals, and roads for the people who work for these companies.
pages.brief: Worshipers pray inside a mosque in Dubai. Outside, women wear dark robes and head scarves, while men and women use head coverings as a sign of respect. Around them, city buildings, schools, hospitals, and roads serve the growing population along the coast.

pages.text: Landforms of the United Arab Emirates Almost all of the land in the UAE is desert. Land On the coast, the UAE is hot. In the east, the Hajar Mountains rise 2,000 meters (6,500 ft.). The country gets very little rainfall. However, the little it gets—10–15 centimeters (4–6 in.) per year— falls in the mountains. But the mountains are just a small part of the UAE. The rest of the UAE is almost entirely made up of desert, which is even hotter. Desert temperatures may reach 49 degrees Celsius (120°F). Winds from the north sometimes carry dust and sand. Some of the world’s largest sand dunes are found in the UAE’s deserts.
pages.brief: The Hajar Mountains rise in the east above hot desert land, with dust and sand carried by northern winds. Beyond the mountains, vast desert stretches out, holding some of the world's largest sand dunes under intense heat.

pages.text: Most of the desert is dry and tough, but an oasis allows some relief. An oasis is a fertile spot in a desert where water is usually found and plants and animals may live. The largest oasis, Al Ain, lies in the middle of the city of Al Ain about 160 kilometers (100 mi.) east of Abu Dhabi. Oasis with palm trees In the desert, plant life is limited to thin grasses and bushes. But in an oasis, date palms, alfalfa, mangoes, and other crops grow. These spots also support desert animals, including the Arabian oryx, Gordon’s wildcat, sand fox, and sand and mountain gazelles. However, hunting has put some animals in danger. People had to help out to save the Arabian oryx, which is now protected. Arabian Oryx Gordon’s Wildcat Sand Fox Sand Gazelle.
pages.brief: In the desert near Al Ain, an oasis with palm trees and crops gives relief, where date palms, alfalfa, and mangoes grow. Arabian oryx, Gordon's wildcat, sand fox, and gazelles live around the fertile spot, with the oryx now protected.

pages.text: History People have lived on the Arabian Peninsula for thousands of years. Groups settled in the area and began to follow the religion of Islam around 600 ce. In the 1500s, the gulf became a route for ships between Europe and the Far East. The ships carried goods that countries traded. In the 1700s, the Arab states that make up what is today the UAE began to form. These groups fought for control of the gulf. Sometimes they attacked British trade ships. Britain fought back, took control of the area, and made peace with the sheikhs, or leaders. In 1820 the sheikhs agreed to stop fighting at sea. In the mid-1900s one sheikh allowed British oil companies to look at the land. In 1958, one of these companies found oil in Abu Dhabi. The area quickly became wealthy. offshore oil well.
pages.brief: An offshore oil well stands in the gulf, recalling how a British oil company found oil in Abu Dhabi in 1958. In the background, ships once carried trade goods across the gulf between Europe and the Far East.

pages.text: Each year on December 2, fireworks displays add excitement to National Day—the day the UAE celebrates its independence from Great Britain. In the years to follow, oil was also found in other states. Oil companies quickly began drilling and soon discovered that the area held more oil and natural gas than most other places in the world. In 1968, Britain left and the states decided to form a federation. Six Arab states formed the UAE in 1971. The final seventh state joined in 1972. The Trucial States had gained independence from Britain. When war broke out in 1980 with the neighboring countries of Iran and Iraq, fighting put ships loaded with oil in danger in the gulf. The UAE, along with several other middle eastern countries, joined the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) in 1981 to keep the area safe.
pages.brief: Fireworks light the sky over a National Day celebration, marking the UAE's independence from Great Britain. Offshore, oil ships and drilling equipment recall the country's oil wealth and the regional effort to keep gulf shipping safe.

pages.text: Landmarks Palaces and flashy tourist attractions make up the things to see in the United Arab Emirates. The Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque is one of the most beautiful UAE landmarks. Sheikh Zayed helped make money for the UAE while celebrating its culture. The mosque is a symbol of Islam, which teaches respect, love, and peace. Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque Emirates Palace, though not home to royalty, is a landmark of Arab culture. In a city marked by fancy hotels, the palace stands out. It stands on 85 hectares (210 acres) of beautifully cared-for garden space. The palace holds 348 rooms and 14 world- class restaurants for its guests. Burj Khalifa At 830 meters (2,723 ft.) tall, the Burj Khalifa skyscraper in Dubai sets the record as the tallest building in the world. Unlike the Grand Mosque or Emirates Palace, Burj Khalifa is entirely modern. It stands for all that is possible for the future of Dubai. The Burj Khalifa tower took six years to build. It opened in 2010.
pages.brief: The Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque rises with white domes, a beautiful landmark symbolizing Islam's teachings of respect, love, and peace. Nearby, Emirates Palace stands among cared-for gardens, while the Burj Khalifa tower in Dubai reaches far above the city as the world's tallest building.

pages.text: Another record-breaking landmark in Dubai is Palm Jumeirah—one of the world’s largest human- made islands. From above, it looks like a palm tree. First billed as the eighth wonder of the world, this tourist spot includes four thousand houses. Parks and ski areas are common tourist spots in most places, but the fact that they exist at all in this desert country makes them a landmark. Ferrari World in Abu Dhabi is a huge indoor park. Visitors enjoy rides and drive small cars. Ski Dubai is the first indoor ski area in the Middle East. Skiers enjoy slopes covered with man-made snow. Ferrari World Palm Jumeirah Ski Dubai.
pages.brief: From above, Palm Jumeirah looks like a palm tree, a human-made island with houses and tourist spots in Dubai. Elsewhere, visitors drive small cars at Ferrari World in Abu Dhabi, and skiers enjoy man-made snow slopes at Ski Dubai.

pages.text: Conclusion A small nation in the desert of the Arabian peninsula, the UAE is a booming country. Since the discovery of oil, the country has become rich. More people want to move there to work in this exciting industry. With so many people arriving, the culture has changed as well. Modern citizens are proud of their country’s success while still holding onto their Arabic past. The UAE will certainly continue to grow. An old Dubai Mosque sits among modern skyscrapers. Together, they show the respect for tradition and excitement for the future.
pages.brief: An old Dubai mosque sits among modern skyscrapers, showing respect for tradition beside excitement for the future. The small desert nation has grown rich since oil was found, drawing people from many places while citizens remain proud of their Arabic past.

pages.text: United Arab Emirates Population: 5,927,482 Land: 83,600 sq km (32,278 sq. mi.) Capital City: Abu Dhabi Primary Language: Arabic Primary Religion: Islam Name of Currency: UAE dirham.
pages.brief: Abu Dhabi, the capital city of the UAE, stands beside the gulf. The country has a population of about 5,927,482 people and a land area of 83,600 square kilometers; Arabic is the primary language, Islam the primary religion, and the UAE dirham the currency.

books.title: April Fools' Day
books.art_why: The book covers ancient, medieval, and modern events, so drawings can show historical and playful scenes consistently.

pages.text: April Fools’ Day.
pages.brief: A bright springtime title scene for April Fools’ Day, with smiling children and adults sharing harmless jokes outdoors. A saltshaker, paper fish, and fake spider suggest playful pranks, while the cheerful mood introduces a book about the holiday’s history and customs.

pages.text: A common April Fools’ joke is to loosen the top on a saltshaker. Pranking Fun It’s early spring. Your chili ends up buried under a pile of salt. You’ve been the victim of an April Fools’ joke. April Fools’ Day is celebrated on or around the first day of April every year. It’s one day of the year when it’s okay to play jokes, or pranks, on people.
pages.brief: A person at a table reacts as a loosened saltshaker dumps a thick layer of salt over a bowl of chili. Nearby, a friend grins after setting up the harmless April Fools’ prank, with spring flowers suggesting early April.

pages.text: Popular pranks might be to put grease on a doorknob or swap the sugar for salt. You might get friends to do something silly, like try to buy plaid paint. When they realize it’s a joke, it’s traditional to shout “April Fools’!” April Fools’ Day.
pages.brief: A doorknob shines with grease while a person reaches for it. Nearby, a sugar bowl has been swapped with salt, and two friends try to buy plaid paint at a shop. When they realize the joke, they shout with laughter.

pages.text: Why April First? No one knows why April Fools’ Day is on April 1. The holiday may have originally had to do with welcoming spring. Many were often “fooled” by the changing weather at this time of the year. Another idea is that April Fools’ Day began in the 1500s when the calendar we use today was introduced. The start of the new year was moved from the beginning of April to January 1. People who still celebrated New Year’s Day on the first of April were called “April fools.” Gotham Goes Mad One story tells how April Fools’ may have started in the English town of Gotham. King John planned to take villagers’ land and property. The villagers acted as though they suffered from insanity to scare King John away. In those days, insanity was thought to be contagious. One of the villagers’ tricks was to tie a “sick” wheelbarrow to a tree to stop it from biting anyone!
pages.brief: A spring landscape shows changing weather, then a calendar shifts New Year from April to January. In the town of Gotham, villagers act wildly to scare King John away, tying a wheelbarrow to a tree as if it were sick.

pages.text: “Washing the Lions” was a fake event staged at the Tower of London in England. No actual lions were present. Many cultures in the past held celebrations near April 1. The ancient Romans celebrated the longer days of spring. They dressed in costumes and played games and jokes. At the end of the twelfth century, people celebrated the Feast of Fools in parts of Europe. People chose a false ruler to lead the celebrations. The followers joined in the fun by dressing in disguise. People celebrated in this way until the sixteenth century. April Fools’ Day.
pages.brief: At the Tower of London, a crowd gathers for a fake lion-washing event with no real lions. In another scene, ancient Romans in costumes enjoy spring games and jokes, while a Feast of Fools celebration shows a pretend ruler leading disguised followers.

pages.text: Around the World Today, people celebrate April Fools’ Day differently around the world. Scottish Scramble Some people in parts of the United Kingdom believe that the fun must stop by noon. In Scotland, however, April Fools’ can go on for two days. On April 1, some people send friends on foolish errands. The second day is for playing more jokes. Tips to Avoid Being the April Fool! • Have you read it carefully? Do you really believe there is a cross between a sheep and a pig called a “shig?” • Do you get the feeling you’re being watched? Be on your guard! • Careful! That present may not be what you think. Scotland ATLANTIC OCEAN.
pages.brief: In Scotland, people send friends on foolish errands and keep the jokes going for a second day. A map shows Scotland beside the Atlantic Ocean. Nearby, a suspicious present and a strange sheep-pig creature hint at tricks, while someone feels watched and stays on guard.

pages.text: “April Fish” is also celebrated in other parts of Europe and Canada. French Foolishness In France, April 1 is often known as “April Fish.” The fish is a person who is easily caught, or easily fooled. A paper fish is taped to the victim’s back. April Fools’ Day 10 ATLANTIC OCEAN France.
pages.brief: In France, a person walks unaware with a paper fish taped to their back. Friends nearby smile at the April Fish trick. A map places France beside the Atlantic Ocean, and the scene shows the playful custom of fooling someone who is easily caught.

pages.text: American Tricksters In the United States, the fun lasts all day. Telling a friend that class is canceled and punching holes in his or her water bottle are examples of common pranks. Other pranks are putting oil on a doorknob and adding food coloring to someone’s milk. Another trick is putting plastic bugs on food, beds, or chairs! Canada United States PACIFIC OCEAN Brazil Brazil’s Day of the Lie In Brazil, April 1 is Dia da mentira (Lie Day). People enjoy playing practical jokes, or brincadeiras (breen-kah- DAY-rahs), on each other and tell silly lies all day.
pages.brief: In the United States, a student hears that class is canceled while a water bottle leaks from tiny holes. Other pranks include oil on a doorknob, colored milk, and plastic bugs on food, beds, and chairs. In Brazil, people tell silly lies all day, with a map showing Canada, the United States, and Brazil.

pages.text: Jordanian Jokesters On April 1, 2010, a newspaper in Jordan had an interesting front-page story. It reported that three spaceships had landed in the desert outside a town in eastern Jordan. Some people in the town were not used to April Fools’ pranks and were really scared. The mayor considered evacuating the thirteen thousand people who lived there. The newspaper’s editor apologized for the story. Iran Jordan Sizdah Bedar The Iranian (Persian) calendar is very old and is only used in Iran and Afghanistan. The thirteenth day of the Iranian new year is called Sizdah Bedar (seez-DAH be-DAR). It falls around April 1 and has been practiced since 536 bc. On Sizdah Bedar, families and friends share picnics, pranks, and fun. It might just be the oldest-known joke day in history. April Fools’ Day.
pages.brief: In Jordan, villagers react with fear to a newspaper story about three spaceships landing in the desert, and the mayor considers evacuating thirteen thousand people. In Iran, families and friends share a picnic with pranks and fun for Sizdah Bedar. A map shows Iran and Jordan.

pages.text: BBC TV’s show Panorama showed a family from Switzerland during its annual “spaghetti harvest.” Famous Foolery Famous April Fools’ celebrations have also made their mark on history. Spaghetti Trees? In 1957, a British TV program told viewers about a spaghetti tree. Viewers were shown people pulling spaghetti from trees. After the program, hundreds of viewers called the station asking how to grow their own spaghetti trees!
pages.brief: A British television program shows a Swiss family during a spaghetti harvest. Viewers watch people pulling long strands of spaghetti from trees. After the broadcast, hundreds of callers ask the station how they can grow their own spaghetti trees.

pages.text: Corporate Chaos Companies and the media release fake stories, too. On April 1, 1996, Taco Bell announced that it had bought the Liberty Bell, the famous American treasure. The company said it was going to call it the “Taco Liberty Bell.” Many people believed the story. The company then had to state that it was a joke. Liberty Bell In 1998, Burger King published an ad for a left-handed burger. The company claimed it was created to make left-handed eating easier. Can you tell the difference between a left-handed and right-handed burger? April Fools’ Day.
pages.brief: Taco Bell announces it has bought the Liberty Bell and will rename it the Taco Liberty Bell, while people react with surprise. A Burger King advertisement shows a left-handed burger made for easier left-handed eating, and diners inspect it closely to spot the difference.

pages.text: Online Pranks Online April Fools’ jokes spread quickly. Google is well known for its April Fools’ jokes. One of its most famous jokes was the Google Gulp in 2005. The Google Gulp was a drink that was said to make the person who drank it smarter. In 2012, a radio station announced that Twitter was changing to 133 characters per tweet. This would save the company $1.4 billion. It wasn’t true, of course. On April 1, 2013, Twitter said it would start charging more to people if they used vowels in their tweets. If people wanted to use vowels, they could pay extra every month. Even the idea for Pokémon Go began as an Internet joke in 2014. Google Maps advertised a tool that would find the world’s best Pokémon Master. To catch a creature in the April Fools’ version of Pokémon Go, just tap the screen.
pages.brief: A person drinks a fictional Google Gulp, said to make the drinker smarter. A radio station announces a shorter tweet limit, and Twitter jokes about charging extra for vowels. On a phone screen, a player taps to catch a creature in an early Pokémon Go joke.

pages.text: Conclusion Follow certain safety rules when celebrating April Fools’ Day. Don’t be mean. April Fools’ jokes are supposed to be fun. Finally, remember that if you’re going to make a joke, make sure you can take a joke in return. On April Fools’ Day in many countries around the world, jokers try to fool the unsuspecting. It is one special day to celebrate the funny side of life. Keep it safe and simple and, most of all, fun. April Fools’ Day.
pages.brief: A group of friends share a safe, simple April Fools’ joke and laugh together. One person makes a playful prank while another smiles and takes the joke well. The scene shows that jokes should be kind, harmless, and fun for everyone involved.

books.title: Jackie Robinson
books.art_why: A named famous person biography.

pages.text: Introduction African Americans play a big part in professional sports today. For many years, however, black athletes weren’t allowed to play with white athletes. One African American— Jackie Robinson— changed all that. His courage made him a baseball hero and a champion for equal rights.
pages.brief: Jackie Robinson in a baseball uniform stands at the center of a modern stadium, while African American athletes play professional sports in the background, showing how he opened doors and became a champion for equal rights.

pages.text: The Early Years Jack Roosevelt Robinson was born into a poor Georgia family in 1919. In college, he was a star on his school’s football, track, basketball, and baseball teams. His family had little money, however. He left college in 1941 to help support his family and did not finish school.
pages.brief: Young Jack Roosevelt Robinson stands with his family outside a modest Georgia home, then appears as a college athlete in football, track, basketball, and baseball uniforms, showing his star performances before he left school in 1941 to help support his family.

pages.text: Taking a Stand In December 1941, the United States entered a war. Like many young men at the time, Robinson was called up to serve in the U.S. Army. One day, he and a group of soldiers got on an army bus. The bus was segregated. White soldiers sat in the front and black soldiers in the back. Yet Robinson knew he was as good a soldier as the white men. He would not move to the back. Robinson was arrested, but many people defended him. He was a good soldier who had only stood up for what was right. In the end, he was found not guilty.
pages.brief: In a segregated Army bus, Jackie Robinson in uniform stands firm near the front while white soldiers sit ahead and black soldiers sit behind; outside a military courtroom, people defend him as he is found not guilty.

pages.text: You’re Hired! After his time in the army, Robinson played baseball. In 1945, however, baseball was segregated, too. White and black athletes played in separate leagues. Robinson felt that baseball leagues should not be separate based on race. So did Branch Rickey, the man who ran the Brooklyn Dodgers. Rickey wanted the Dodgers to be the first white team to include a black player. Rickey knew that this player would not only have to be a great athlete. He would also have to face abuse because of his race.
pages.brief: Branch Rickey, the man who ran the Brooklyn Dodgers, stands in a team office while Jackie Robinson plays baseball in a segregated league; Rickey knows the first black player on a white team must be a great athlete and face abuse.

pages.text: Rickey hired Robinson. He had one condition, though. Robinson could not respond to any of the abuse. Instead, Robinson would fight prejudice by playing great baseball. A Team of Two A Team of Two.
pages.brief: Branch Rickey and Jackie Robinson sit across from each other in a Brooklyn Dodgers office, making their agreement; Rickey raises one finger to show the condition that Robinson must not answer abuse and will fight prejudice by playing great baseball.

pages.text: Number 42 Takes the Field Jackie Robinson began by playing for the Dodgers’ minor league team. On the road, he could not stay in the same hotels as the rest of the team. Other minor league teams would not play because of Robinson. Pitchers on other teams threw the ball at him. Even some of the men on his own team didn’t want to play with him.
pages.brief: Jackie Robinson, wearing a minor league Dodgers uniform, stands alone outside a hotel while his white teammates go inside; on the field, an opposing pitcher throws a ball toward him and teammates turn away, showing the abuse he faced on the road.

pages.text: None of this abuse stopped Robinson. He played well enough to move up to the Dodgers the next year. Wearing number 42, he took the field on April 15, 1947, before a crowd of twenty-six thousand people.
pages.brief: Jackie Robinson in a Brooklyn Dodgers uniform with number 42 on his back steps onto the field at a packed baseball stadium on April 15, 1947, before a crowd of twenty-six thousand spectators, showing his historic debut.

pages.text: The stands were full when Robinson picked up his baseball bat. The crowd watched as he walked to the plate. Insults rang out from the other team’s dugout. The words hurt, but Robinson did not respond. He let his bat do the talking.
pages.brief: Jackie Robinson holds his baseball bat at the plate in front of packed stands while players in the opposing dugout shout insults at him; he keeps his face calm and does not respond, ready to let his bat do the talking.

pages.text: The Dodgers earned a victory that day, not only over Boston but also over prejudice. Robinson forced many people who thought less of African Americans to think again. Another Great Steal Another Great Steal.
pages.brief: Jackie Robinson steals a base during a Dodgers game against Boston, kicking up dust as the crowd watches; his play helps the Dodgers win and makes people who thought less of African Americans think again.

pages.text: Robinson went on to have a great career. In 1949, he was voted Most Valuable Player in the league. He was a fast runner who led the league in stolen bases. In 1962, Robinson became the first African American to get into the Baseball Hall of Fame.
pages.brief: Jackie Robinson sprints to steal another base in a Dodgers uniform, while a later scene shows him as the first African American inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1962 after being named Most Valuable Player in 1949.

pages.text: His Number, His Day His Number, His Day.
pages.brief: Jackie Robinson stands at a ceremony in a baseball stadium while a large number 42 is displayed on the field and fans celebrate a special day in his honor, remembering his number and his lasting place in baseball history.

pages.text: Beyond Baseball After Robinson stopped playing baseball in 1957, he went into business. He became the first black vice president of a U.S. national company. He also became a civil rights leader. He continued to work for equal rights for all people until his death in 1972. Today in the United States, more people of color play in the world of sports than ever before. We all have Number 42 to thank for that. Robinson helped run the coffee maker Chock Full o’ Nuts. Here, he works at his desk in January 1962.
pages.brief: Jackie Robinson, in a suit, sits at his desk in a January 1962 office at Chock Full o’ Nuts, focused on his business work; the scene shows him after baseball as a company vice president and civil rights leader.

books.title: A Crafty Escape
books.art_why: Nineteenth-century escape events and slavery scenes predate reliable photographs, so drawings are appropriate.

pages.text: Introduction Dressing in costume as someone else can be entertaining and fun. Now imagine that your life depends on how well you play that part. In the nineteenth century, that was the case for the Crafts. They disguised themselves to escape being enslaved. People as Property The Crafts, like all Black enslaved people in nineteenth-century America, were considered property. They were forced to do whatever their enslavers wanted them to do. They had none of the rights enjoyed by white people. They were not allowed to learn how to read or write. They could be bought and sold. They also could be starved, beaten, or even killed if they angered their enslavers. In January 1863, President Lincoln signed the Emancipation Proclamation, which granted freedom to many, but not all, enslaved people. The original proclamation freed those enslaved in most slaveholding states. It did not pertain to Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, and Missouri. The enslaved people in those states would have to wait two more years to be free.
pages.brief: In a nineteenth-century American setting, a Black couple, the Crafts, wear disguises to escape slavery. In another scene, President Lincoln signs the Emancipation Proclamation in January 1863. Enslaved people in several states remain unfree and must wait two more years.

pages.text: Born into Slavery William and Ellen Craft were Black Americans born into slavery. William, born in 1824, lived in Macon, Georgia. His family was owned by a man who liked to gamble. To settle his debts, the man sold off the members of William’s family, one at a time. William was sold when he was sixteen years old. He had been working as a carpenter and was quite skilled. His new enslaver realized that he could gain a good income from William’s skills. He had William continue to work as a cabinetmaker and earn money for him. Ellen was two years younger than William. Her father was a white man who enslaved Ellen’s mother. Ellen’s skin was very light, and people didn’t suspect her mother was Black. At the age of eleven, Ellen was “given” to her newly married half sister to do the work of a servant. Ellen moved to Macon with her half sister’s family. There, she eventually met William. Ellen Craft William Craft.
pages.brief: Young William Craft works as a skilled carpenter and cabinetmaker in Macon, Georgia, before being sold at sixteen. In another view, young Ellen Craft, whose skin is very light, moves to Macon as a servant for her half sister’s family. Ellen later meets William there.

pages.text: A Decision Fueled by Love William and Ellen fell in love and wanted to be together, but marriages between enslaved people were complicated. They needed their enslavers’ permission to wed. If enslaved couples had different enslavers, the couple could not live together. In 1846, Ellen and William got permission and were married. For two years, they lived apart, seeing each other only occasionally. Being apart was hard for the Crafts. They knew that one of them could be sold at any time and sent far away from the other.
pages.brief: William and Ellen Craft stand together in Macon, Georgia, after receiving permission from their enslavers to marry in 1846. For two years they live apart, seeing each other only occasionally. Both worry that one of them could be sold and sent far away.

pages.text: The Crafts realized that the only way they could live as a family would be to escape and flee north. Black people could live freely in the Northern states. But how could the Crafts do it without being caught? Fortunately, they had a plan. Free States and Slave States In 1860, there were thirty-three states in the United States. Slavery was legal in the fifteen Southern “slave states” and illegal in the eighteen Northern “free states.” In the states where slavery was legal, enslaved Black people had none of the rights of their white enslavers. In free states, Black people could live as free citizens. The slave states seceded from the United States to form the Confederacy. After the Confederates lost the Civil War, the Thirteenth Amendment to the Constitution abolished slavery in the United States, and all states became free states. Slavery in States and Territories, 1860.
pages.brief: The Crafts, a young Black couple, make a plan to flee north to a free state. A map of the United States in 1860 shows fifteen Southern slave states and eighteen Northern free states. The couple hopes to live freely without being caught.

pages.text: Preparing and Planning The Crafts came up with a daring scheme. They would travel to Pennsylvania, the nearest free state. Because Ellen’s skin was so light, she would pretend to be a white person. William could travel with her as her loyal house servant. There was just one problem—Ellen could not travel as a woman. Women of that era did not travel alone, and they certainly didn’t travel with an enslaved man. There was only one way their plan would work. Ellen had to travel disguised as a white man.
pages.brief: The Crafts plan a daring journey to Pennsylvania, the nearest free state. Ellen, whose skin is light, will pretend to be a white person. William will travel beside her as her loyal house servant. Ellen must disguise herself as a white man because women did not travel alone.

pages.text: Ellen was fearful at first. If they were caught, they would be harshly punished. She finally agreed when they decided how her disguise would work. The night of the escape, William would cut her hair short. She would wear special undergarments to hide her figure. She would also wear a bandage around her face and green spectacles. These would hide her smooth skin and womanly features. To complete the disguise, Ellen would wear one arm in a sling. Ellen was never allowed to learn to read or write. An injured arm would give her the perfect excuse not to have to sign her name for tickets. Traveling as a sick person would also explain William’s presence as a good servant helping his enslaver. As long as they acted their parts, no one would suspect a thing.
pages.brief: At night, William cuts Ellen’s hair short and helps her into her disguise. Ellen wears special undergarments, a bandage around her face, green spectacles, and one arm in a sling. The disguise hides her smooth skin and womanly features and explains why she cannot sign her name.

pages.text: The Great Escape Begins The Crafts decided to leave on December 21, 1848. William had been hiding money from his cabinetmaking for their trip. The couple asked their enslavers for some time off for Christmas. Time off was often given to enslaved people at Christmas to celebrate with their families. The Crafts could leave and not be missed until they were long gone. When the day came, William cut Ellen’s hair and helped her into her costume. They both said a prayer and went into town to buy train tickets to Savannah, Georgia. Travel at that time was segregated, so they boarded separate train cars. Then they sat and waited to begin their trip. The Crafts’ Escape Route December 21–25, 1848 Boston, Massachusetts Pennsylvania ATLANTIC OCEAN Maryland Washington, D.C. North Carolina South Carolina United States England Macon, Georgia Boston.
pages.brief: On December 21, 1848, William cuts Ellen’s hair and helps her dress. They pray, then go into town to buy train tickets to Savannah, Georgia. William and Ellen board separate train cars because travel is segregated. They sit and wait for their trip to begin.

pages.text: Suddenly, William noticed a familiar face on the train platform. It was the owner of the cabinetmaking shop where William worked! The man thought William might be fleeing with his wife and began walking through the train, searching for them. William crouched down in his seat, shaking with fear. Just as the man reached William’s car, the departure bell clanged. The man left, and William sighed in relief—he was safe. Ellen, sitting in another train car, had a scare of her own. When her seatmate arrived, Ellen recognized him as a good friend of her enslaver. This man was someone who had known Ellen for years. Ellen sat very still and did not dare look up. Luckily, her disguise was so convincing that the man greeted her and sat down without a second look. Ellen pretended to be deaf so she could avoid talking and giving herself away.
pages.brief: On the train platform, William sees the owner of the cabinetmaking shop where he worked. The man searches the train for William and Ellen. William crouches in his seat, shaking, until the departure bell rings. In another car, Ellen’s seatmate is her enslaver’s friend, so she pretends to be deaf.

pages.text: Setting Sail for Freedom The Crafts reached Savannah safely and boarded a steamer ship for Charleston, South Carolina. When they arrived in Charleston and tried to buy tickets to Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, however, they ran into trouble. The clerk refused to sign for the couple’s tickets despite Ellen’s apparent “injury.” Luckily, the boat captain from their first ship passed by. He vouched for the pair, and soon they were on their way north again. They met their final hurdle in Baltimore, Maryland. Slave states that shared borders with free states had border patrols. These patrols checked for escapees. The Maryland border patrol stopped the Crafts and demanded proof of William’s ownership. Of course, William and Ellen had no such paperwork. They feared their quest for freedom was over. When the boarding bell sounded, one officer took pity on the pair. He ordered the conductor to let them board. The Crafts arrived safely in Philadelphia on Christmas morning. They found friends and shelter in the home of an abolitionist.
pages.brief: The Crafts reach Savannah and board a steamer ship for Charleston, South Carolina. In Charleston, a clerk refuses to sign their tickets until their first boat captain vouches for them. In Baltimore, Maryland, border patrol officers stop them and demand proof of William’s ownership. An officer takes pity, and they reach Philadelphia on Christmas morning.

pages.text: Across the Ocean to Safety Three weeks after arriving in Philadelphia, the Crafts went on to Boston, Massachusetts. William got a job as a cabinetmaker, and Ellen worked as a seamstress. For a while, life was good for the Crafts. Their happiness did not last, however. In 1850, Congress passed the Fugitive Slave Act. The act made it a crime to protect escapees, even in free states. Law officers could receive a large reward for capturing and returning escapees to their enslavers. The Underground Railroad How did the Crafts know where to go once they reached Philadelphia? The Underground Railroad steered them in the right direction. The Underground Railroad was a system of escape routes and safe houses run by people who helped escapees get to freedom. The routes ran through free Northern states all the way to Canada. Abolitionists knew to keep an eye out for Black people coming into free states from the South. They would provide these newcomers with shelter, food, and directions to freedom.
pages.brief: Three weeks after Philadelphia, the Crafts reach Boston, Massachusetts. William works as a cabinetmaker and Ellen as a seamstress. In 1850, Congress passes the Fugitive Slave Act, making it a crime to protect escapees. A view of the Underground Railroad shows escape routes and safe houses leading from Southern slavery to free Northern states and Canada.

pages.text: Two bounty hunters arrived in Boston, determined to bring the Crafts back to Georgia. The terrified Crafts hid with friends, but they could not bear to live in fear. In December 1850, they set out on another journey, this time to England. The Bloodhound Law In 1850, Congress passed the Fugitive Slave Act. This law stated that a person who helped an escapee would be fined $1,000—a large sum in those days. Anyone who returned an enslaved person to their enslaver would get a reward, or bounty. The law was known as the Bloodhound Law because bounty hunters would use bloodhound dogs to track down escapees. This federal law affected both free and slave states. Still, many free states refused to actively hunt down escapees or the people who helped them.
pages.brief: Two bounty hunters arrive in Boston, determined to bring the Crafts back to Georgia. The terrified couple hides with friends. In December 1850, William and Ellen set out on another journey across the ocean to England. A separate scene shows the 1850 Fugitive Slave Act, known as the Bloodhound Law, with bloodhound dogs tracking escapees.

pages.text: The Long Trip Home The Crafts settled in West London and had five children. They gave lectures against slavery throughout Great Britain. In 1860, William published a book about their escape. The Crafts became teachers, ran a boarding house, and went into business to support their family. In 1870, several years after slavery had ended in the United States, William and Ellen returned to their homeland. They settled outside Savannah, Georgia, purchased a farm, and founded two schools for Black people. However, the end of slavery didn’t meant the end of the Crafts’ struggles against an unjust society. White people who opposed equal rights for Black people burned down those schools. In 1873 the Crafts started another school in Georgia. Anger and harassment by white people forced them to close it down. Afterwards, the Crafts lost their land because no bank would loan them the money they needed for their farm. In 1890 they moved in with a daughter and lived with her until they died. In the end, they achieved what they wanted most from life. They raised a family that could not be torn apart by slavery and lived out their lives—together.
pages.brief: The Crafts settle in West London and raise five children. They give lectures against slavery across Great Britain, and William publishes a book about their escape in 1860. After slavery ends, they return to Georgia, buy a farm, and start schools for Black people. Hostile white people burn the schools, and the Crafts later live with a daughter.

books.title: Wimbledon
books.art_why: Wimbledon is a real modern sports event with real players, places and historical photographs available; it is not about one named famous person.

pages.text: The Magic of Wimbledon It is July 1980. The crowd watches as two tennis titans meet on the well-worn grass of Wimbledon’s center court. It is the ice-cool calm of Swede Björn (BYORN) Borg against the fire and temper of American John McEnroe. Wearing their trademark headbands, both are ready for battle. Borg pounds balls into the corners of the grass court. The balls raise clouds of dust as they hit the chalk lines. McEnroe clutches his curly hair in despair. For nearly four hours, both players give this match everything they have. One commentator shouts, “If this were a heavyweight boxing contest, they would stop the fight!” In the end, it is Borg who holds high the Wimbledon Championship trophy. It is perhaps the most coveted of all tennis prizes. Björn Borg drops to his knees in joy after winning Wimbledon in 1980.
pages.brief: On Wimbledon’s worn center court in July 1980, Björn Borg and John McEnroe face each other in their trademark headbands. Borg pounds balls into the corners, raising dust from the chalk lines, while McEnroe clutches his curly hair in despair. After nearly four hours, Borg drops to his knees in joy and holds high the championship trophy.

pages.text: Wimbledon is the oldest tennis competition in the world. It’s also the name of a leafy area of London, home to the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club, where the tournament started and still takes place each year. It is the only major tournament that hosts the sport on its original surface: grass. All the top professional tennis players in the world want to play there. Winning Wimbledon can turn a tennis player into a tennis legend. For two weeks every June, almost half a million fans attend the matches. Many millions more follow the action on social media and TV. Wimbledon fans love its old-fashioned image of “tennis in an English country garden.” Tennis fans attend a Wimbledon championship final with a sense of awe. They feel the thrill of the players’ nerves when the umpire calls “Time!” and the match begins. They watch the athletes’ feet spring silently on the well-tended lawn courts as they chase the ball. Members of the crowd ooh and aah over their favorite players. Wimbledon fans model their fancy tennis hats. All these things make up the magic of Wimbledon.
pages.brief: A leafy London setting shows the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club, where almost half a million fans attend Wimbledon each June. On the well-tended lawn courts, athletes’ feet spring silently as they chase the ball; the umpire calls “Time!” to begin a match, and the crowd oohs and aahs over favorite players while wearing fancy tennis hats.

pages.text: Wimbledon History Tennis was first played in France about nine hundred years ago. Back then, people used their hands in place of rackets. The rules of the modern game were set in England in the 1870s. People played with a rubber ball on grass. The first Wimbledon Championship was held in 1877 on one of the lawns at the All England Club. The club hoped to raise money to pay for the care of its lawns. The championship really caught the public’s interest in 1889. That’s when Willie Renshaw won the first of six Wimbledon victories in a row. Fans loved his fine serves and overhead smashes. He won three singles championships against his twin brother, Ernest. Together, they won five doubles championships. Willie (left) and Ernest (right) dominated Wimbledon in the 1880s. Twin Win It would take more than a century for two sisters to beat the Renshaw doubles record, but they finally did. In 2016, Venus and Serena Williams won the Wimbledon doubles title for the sixth time. Serena (left) and Venus (right) celebrate after their 2012 win.
pages.brief: Willie and Ernest Renshaw play tennis on a grass lawn, while Serena and Venus Williams celebrate a modern Wimbledon doubles victory. The scene links the first 1877 championship, held to raise money for lawn care, with the sisters’ sixth doubles title in 2016, more than a century after the Renshaw twins dominated Wimbledon.

pages.text: By the 1900s, Wimbledon was attracting players from beyond England. In 1905, May Sutton from the United States became the first international player to win the women’s singles. Australian Norman Brookes became the first international men’s champion in 1907. In 1922, the British royal family gained their own spectators ’ box at Wimbledon. Four years later the Duke of York, who later became King George VI, competed in the men’s doubles. He and his partner lost their match, but to this day players still bow or curtsy to the king or queen.
pages.brief: May Sutton and Norman Brookes stand on a grass court as early international champions, while the British royal family watches from its own spectators’ box. The Duke of York, later King George VI, plays men’s doubles and loses; to this day, players bow or curtsy to the king or queen at Wimbledon.

pages.text: Only top- ranked amateur players could enter Wimbledon until 1968. That year, prize money was awarded for the first time, and it became a tournament for professionals. By 2017, the winners of the men’s and women’s singles competitions each collected close to $3 million. That’s a big paycheck! Do You Know? The four Grand Slams are the most important competitions on the tennis calendar. Players travel from around the world and compete against each other to reach a grand final at the end. The four Grand Slam tournaments are the Australian Open, Wimbledon, the French Open, and the U.S. Open. Winning these titles means fame, and that often means extra money since companies use winning players to help sell products.
pages.brief: A professional tennis player holds a trophy beside a large prize-money cheque on a grass court; four Grand Slam tournaments—the Australian Open, Wimbledon, the French Open and the U.S. Open—are shown around the scene. Winning these titles brings fame and extra money as companies use winning players to sell products.

pages.text: Rules and Traditions Above all other Wimbledon traditions is the grass court. It must be just right. A year-round grounds crew makes sure all twenty grass courts are ready. Every day during the tournament, the grounds crew mow the courts. They keep the height of the grass at exactly 8 millimeters (0.3 in.)—the perfect height for playing. They paint the chalk lines and spray a precise amount of water on the grass at night to help it last. Grass-Court Tennis For players who are not used to playing on real grass, it can be tricky at first. The balls bounce extremely low. Players have to bend their knees more than usual. That’s hard work! As the grass gets more worn, the risk of a “bad bounce” of the ball also increases. Still, some players love playing on grass because it means a faster-bouncing ball. A member of the Wimbledon grounds crew checks court measurements.
pages.brief: A grounds crew member kneels on a grass court to check its measurements while another mows the lawn to exactly eight millimeters; fresh chalk lines are painted and water is sprayed at night. Nearby, a player bends low to reach a ball that bounces low on the worn grass.

pages.text: Three girls enjoy the Wimbledon tradition of strawberries and cream. No advertising is allowed around the courts, and while players can wear whatever color they want in other tournaments, Wimbledon has a strict all-white dress code for its players. It includes shirt collars, cap brims, and even the bottoms of shoes. Eating strawberries and cream at Wimbledon is another tradition. On average, 34,000 kilograms (74,957 lb.) of strawberries and 10,000 liters (2,642 gal.) of cream are sold at each Wimbledon Championship. Another special tradition is the “queue,” the British term for a line of waiting people. Fans can buy passes to walk around the Wimbledon grounds and stand next to an outside court to watch their favorite player practice or compete. Some fans queue all night, hoping to buy a ticket for a certain match. There is even a place for die-hard fans to pitch their tents!
pages.brief: Three girls enjoy strawberries and cream beside a grass court; a player wears a strict all-white outfit with collared shirt, cap brim and white shoe bottoms. In the background, fans queue overnight in a long line, and some pitch tents near the Wimbledon grounds.

pages.text: Famous Finals The men’s and women’s singles competitions contain 128 spots each. A draw determines who plays whom, but the draw isn’t completely random. It spreads out top-ranked players to make sure they don’t play each other until later in the tournament. The more matches a player has won in past tournaments, the higher the ranking he or she will have. The suspense builds through the contest as players battle to get through each round. As with Borg versus McEnroe, Wimbledon has seen some epic finals through the years.
